Moreover you can choose your own style of play:  Are you a hot-shot fighter pilot, a planetary colonist, a trade mogul, an explorer or a crusader.  If you so desire it, the game doesn't explicitly tell you how to "win"--although, for those players who are achievement-oriented, various game missions are offered to give you some guidance.  I've played over 400 hours, and am still quite into the game.

Reviews.125918:
If you'd asked me at launch, when I pre-ordered the game and was greeted with the game in its state at release - on PS4, no less - or even a couple years later, I would steer you away from this game at enormous speed. 

But there is something to be said about the way Hello Games has maintained this title, and their integrity, by not only not abandoning this project, but by expanding and improving upon it so much so that not only can I not justify a negative review, but I would absolutely recommend this game.

If you want fast action, deep narrative and a next gen gaming experience, then no. This isn't the game for you. But if you appreciate exploration, a rich world - infinite rich worlds - and an emphasis on your nearly limitless freedom, then this game is absolutely for you.

No Man's Sky - at least as of some crucial updates - allows you to explore a practically endless procedurally generated universe with your friends, or solo. You can build bases, Find, upgrade and purchase spaceships, use exo vehicles like submarines, fly freighter ships akin to Star Destroyers, pilot giant mech suits, find living spaceships, and so much more.

I won't lie to you; it can get repetitive. I've played 100+ hours and while I do plan on playing again, as of my last big session I felt I had exhausted the game's available biomes. That is a real problem. 26 trillion or however many worlds there are doesn't mean as much if there are only 30 or 40 variants of those.

But, the game is being constantly updated, and it wouldn't surprise me if this issue as well as any other issues are visited and corrected in the coming months or years.

Buying No Man's Sky is sort of an investment. At the point of writing, in late 2020, it is worth the money and if you're like me, yes, it's 100 hours worth for your money. In the future, it very well might be even better. 

Keep your eye on this, or grab it now. Don't let its bad past dissuade you; No Man's Sky is a good game. And Hello Games have proven themselves to be a trustworthy dev team.

This is a pretty fuckin cool space game but it gets boring very quickly. It's a game with basically unlimited procedurally generated planets and solar systems that you can terraform and mold to your heart's content, and yet planets feel like they lack variety. Visit a dozen or so planets and you've seen half or more of the total procedural generation. There is no variety on different areas of each planet; visit a planet, and your immediate surroundings make up the entirety of the planet - flora, fauna, temperature, biome, everything. If this game makes a lot more progress towards variety in procedural generation, I think it'll improve the game's playability very much.

Expanding on this, the interiors of space stations desperately need variation. Every space station does have a different exterior, which is something, but literally every space station in the game has the exact same copy-paste interior. Mixing it up even to make 2 or 3 different ones would massively improve my attitude towards the game, because I'm visiting space stations pretty often. This is more of a personal thing, but having an old-timey space bar would be badass, gives my eyes a nice break from the constant sci-fi tech shit I see everywhere.

The only real threat in this game is either sentinels, which you can run away from, or fall damage. You're not in any real danger for like 9/10ths of the game.

From my playtime, the game has been very rarely buggy or has had issues, so it plays well.

Personally, I think this game has made leaps and bounds development-wise, but it still needs a big amount of work before I can call it a good game and a game worth playing.

This game does have a lot of potential to be something great. It has a beautiful soundtrack and you can find all sorts of amazing worlds with great scenery. The potential for exploration, constructing settlements and establishing yourself in your own space colony, or one with friends are endless. 

However there are some things that really need to change to make sure this game keeps continuing to attract players. 

For example, the game is way too slow paced and can become very boring to players who have no interest in sitting around mining constantly. 

There aren't as much interesting structures as expected, either constructed or natural to explore as expected. A future update should include larger settlements other than just buildings in the middle of nowhere, perhaps some cities or towns would be great to find and explore when you're on a planet. It would be interesting to find more diverse biomes on a planet and much more places to explore whether it's above ground or underground.  

Space stations are really lacking in depth or detail so it's a bit disappointing when you travel to one and all you find is a few rooms and nothing more. If the space anomaly has expanded to the point that it has become now, it would be great to see the space stations get the same sort of treatment. 

The ability to navigate when your ship is landing on a planet is negatively affected by the controls and lack of information on how fast you're going and how high up you are in the air. A decent altimeter would be great for the ships. 

Creatures are rather one-dimensional in their interactions. All you can really do at this moment is feed them and farm for anything they make like eggs or milk. It would be nice to keep a creature as a pet, beast of burden or as livestock more effectively.

Reviews.126098:
No Man's Sky.  Forever a part of video game history as the most unlikely comeback story in the game industry.  When it first launched, the game was a major disappointment; offering a full-sized galaxy but little to actually do in it.  Procedural generation was sometimes buggy and the gameplay loop of mining resources to charge equipment was too tight to be satisfying.

For the full story, you can look up The Internet Historian's video "The Engoodening Of No Man's Sky" on Youtube. He covers it a lot better and more succinctly than I could.

While the game may have had one of the worst launches in recent memory, The dedication of Hello Games in the years since has borne gorgeous alien fruit, making No Man's Sky into a game worth experiencing.  The first two updates alone went far towards atoning for the notorious sins of omission, and there have been an additional three since that have continued to pump new features into the game.  These updates are starting to slow now, but the game today is radically different from the way it was at launched.  It is much closer to being a promise fulfilled.

Still, there are things you should know before you get into the game.  It is not a fast-paced space sim, nor is it as deep as games like Star Citizen.  The gameplay is geared towards deliberate exploration of the galaxy, giving you the tools to do this at your own pace and providing plenty of options-multiple routes through getting things like credits and upgrades that bring you closer to your goal.  There are a number of technology trees, quest lines, crafting loops and sundry activities to work through, but exploration remains key.  It does not play quite like other video games, and because of this it may not be for everybody.  But I definitely recommend giving it a shot if you are on the fence about it.

After 134 hours I guess I owe this game a review. I'm really torn. The devs did a fantastic job of making a universe that could be explored infinitely. The story is rather blah. The whole game feels like a really nice tech demo but now it needs a game built into it. It needs urgency in some moments. 

There's a lot of stuff in the game that lacks purpose such as fauna on the planets and repairing frigates. I was really hoping the fauna would have more of a feel that the cannibals in the forest had or the dinosaurs on ark.

On the derelict freighters, I was hoping for a little more dead space style intensity to give the game some flavor.

Around 100 hour mark, I got stuck when warping to someone else's base so I had to use a save editor to move my character. At that point, I just cheated and used the save editor for anything I wanted to try out but it didn't feel like cheating, it just felt like saving time.

Multiplayer is a bit odd. The game isn't a true MMO but it's kind of close. The bases you build are stored on the server if you choose to upload them but if two people are working together, the stuff you are building can only be associated at a player level. So if one person starts at one end and the other starts at the other, the power lines and such won't connect when they meet.

I'll give it a recommended as it is worth checking out but you'll quickly realize that it's just the same thing over and over again. Depends how long you can fool yourself into enjoying it. I was able to for quite a while.

Alright, after a 100 hours of playtime and having reached the end of the story, I would advise people not to play this game. It is a pit of frustration, and while it has potential, the sentiment I am left with is simple disgust towards the time and hope I have invested in the game. Base-building is fun, there is a nice variety of planet ; but my god is the story infuriating to follow. Your character apparently has a major in philosophy, most of the dialogues is you pc thinking by himself on things ; his goal is to rescue and follow the instruction of empty shells, for no reward whatsoever. From start to finish I had no idea what was going on, nothing had any impact on me and I regret the time I wasted being curious to see where all of this mumbo-jumbo led me. It led nowhere. Because of this, I simply got increasingly saltier towards this game to the point where I can't possibly trust it to give me a sense that I accomplished anything through the grinding, and this game is nothing but grinding. There is cool stuff to build, beautiful scenery to build it on, exciting vessels to get ; but almost every time inane nonsense gets in the way of the fun. Also now, quicksilver, a vital currency to acquire beautiful things is barely ever existent as a reward, so there is even less choice in personal objectives. Maybe the game will get better in a update or two, but for now, I just want to impersonate something else than a donkey being led with a carrot towards a black hole of boredom and confusion. 

TLDR : Hello Games should hire a proper writer to make something of this mess.

We all know this game got off to a rocky start, but the developers proved they were dedicated to the game, and turned that around. But I have to admit I still struggled with the question "would you recommend this game."

This game really isn't going to be everyone's cup of tea. Everything about the game is both amazing and lacklustre.

The scope of exploration is mind blowing, with some truly amazing sights to see, and yet it very rapidly becomes a "min/maxing" exercise where you are not really seeing anything new, but are just hunting for a planet with a very specific set of stats to call your home.

Combat is... well combat isn't worth mentioning. It is more of an annoyance than a feature.

Collecting ships is somewhat satisfying, though with nearly every ship available to anyone with YouTube or Reddit, I feel the original design goal has fallen apart (e.g. you can't customise the look of your ships, because you are meant to go hunting for the best looking ship you can find... but now that is as easy as opening Reddit).

Base building is fantastic. If you like building bases, I don't really have anything negative to say about base building, particularly with more recent updates.

Over all it is just a very mixed experience, that requires a massive investment of time. And yet, I have put nearly 200 hours in to it and enjoyed myself, so the game is definitely worth the price (and then some) if it is your type of game.

No Man's Sky is not what it was. I played for about 30+ hours at launch and was, like many, disgusted. I didn't return the game as I held out hope they might do something with it; the framework was there for something amazing they just had to put in the time and effort they hadn't before.

Picking it up again now, 4 years later, I can tell you without shadow of a doubt the game is far better than it was; and the seamless drop in drop out multiplayer to hook up with your friends is a cherry on top. 

The way they did navigating back to your base/objective is important too; because why explore really far if it'll take you forever to get back to home. The teleport at your base is how yo u can easily get to it from any space station, and likewise every station has a teleport that you can get to from your base. Little things like the teleport function, the sheer size of the game, and quantity of stuff to do make the core gameplay loop far more fun even if it is still repetitive; because now you have so many different things to look forward to doing, completing, expanding, learning, ect.

All this is to say nothing of the story which while still a bit lack luster so far, is much better than it was and far less buggy.

If you're unsure, catch the game on sale, otherwise I'd say this is a safe outright buy for those who enjoy space exploration and base building.

The only kind of down-side is that a lot of resources seem to be re-used from one planet to the next (at least when it comes to flora).  I haven't branched out far - maybe only 3 galaxies so far - but I've seen a lot of the same plants and animals so far.  Looking forward to seeing what else I can find along the way, though.

That said, there are some downsides - as you've probably heard, the base building is still a bit of a hot mess.  It could be really fun, but the game keeps you in the 3D view to do it.  Would probably have been far better to control more like a blueprinting kind of deal where you could just click/drag your walls and stuff.

Also, there's a weird glitch when you're tunneling where sometimes you'll just randomly teleport back to the surface.

Held off on this one for years. So glad I finally took the plunge.
With so many games to choose from in my library I can honestly say NMS has hooked me like no game has in so long.

Over the past few days
For the first time in what feels like years (and probably has been) I think about this game while I am going to sleep. I think about it when I am not playing, about what I will do when I can play again and wonder about what else there is to discover.

As a player of many survival games and space games this has an intuitive accessibility and yet clear depth to the adventure of it all I am sure I will play this for hundreds of hours to come.

It provides a balanced experience I have sought for so long in a survival/space game that I didn't even know quite what I had been looking for.

I have even introduced it to my 7 year old and 3 year old sons (creative mode) and they are blown away by the scope and scale of it as well as the fact that it is accessible to them as well (within reason)

I am aware of the turbulent launch but I can comfortably say NMS is a title perhaps like none other.
That the developer believed in, and cared for the the extent that they turned it around so significantly 
and with a constant stream of FREE updates.

So many other titles end up abandoned, or lacking so much of what was promised and end up releasing cash grabby or simply overpriced DLC to pad the experience.
Not NMS.

It was obviously a labor of love and it is an honor to play this game in its current state.
Truly remarkable, and may easily end up being one of my new favorite games of all time. 

I wasn't sure about paying the full price (even though I am sure content wise it beats out many other AAA priced games) but since it is so frequently on sale for just over $20 USD it is insanity to deprive your library of this seminal title...

Oh, and though I don't have a VR set it apparently kicks ass with a headset as well.

Final notes?
Runs well on an old gaming laptop with a 2gb GTX 965m
as well as flawlessly on my desktop with much superior hardware.

Do yourself a favor and give it a shot.

I've played No Man's Sky for 160 hours.

After finally spending about 45 hours on a single save instead of starting from scratch, I finally managed to reach the center of the galaxy. My only regret is that there is no achievement to be had for reaching the center in normal mode.

I started my voyage just over 660 lightyears away from the center. I figured I could cover that in 7 jumps. I made a jump... and I was still 660 lightyears away. Then I realized that Hello Games is based in Great Britain... and they use periods where we use commas. So I was actually 660,000 lightyears  away from the center. Ouch.

I eventually got all of the hyperdrive upgrades for my B class Sentinel Mothership (with 7 middle sections), and figured that at 2000 lightyears per jump, I'd need to make 330 jumps. I made 400 warp cells just in case. After 6 hours of hyperspacing, I made it to the center of the galaxy. I only fell through my freighter once, which would be a problem if I was playing on hardcore. I was surprised to find that I ended up only using 326 warp cells, which was remarkably close to my original estimate.

Now, I am about to talk about what happened when I reached the center, and other thoughts from finishing the game. If you have not played the game, do not read what follows. It will ruin your experience if you do.

About reaching the center of the galaxy:
[spoiler]I flew to the center of the galaxy... and all of a sudden, I was in the galaxy loading screen. Some nice music was playing. I was flying backward, out to the edge of the universe. Eventually, there were no stars, and everything faded to black. A new universe faded into view, and the camera was rushing toward the center. Then everything went white and I was on a random world, all alone, starting over.
All my equipment was damaged. I might've continued playing, but the amount of time required
to gather all the parts to fix it made me say "I'm done".

I had read review sites, and they said the end was anticlimactic. I did not expect this. Seriously, a triple-A game title has an ending for which it is obvious no effort was put in? 
Come on Hello Games, you're killing me.[/spoiler]

Now for the big spoiler:
[spoiler]Apparently, the whole universe in No Man's Sky is just a simulation. Gee whiz, I'm playing this thing on a PC. Of course it's a simulation. 

In all seriousness, though, please let [i]The Matrix[/i] be [i]The Matrix[/i]. Although it worked for the scope of No Man's Sky, doing that kind of a thing with a story is still like doing "then I woke up, and it was all a dream."[/spoiler]

On that note, [spoiler]
it does make me wonder... when I found the simulation thingy on the space station, when my 
character saw the face of the Maker of the ATLAS working on the ATLAS terminal... was the face my own, or that of Sean Murray?[/spoiler]

There is one suggestion I would like to make to Hello Games: 
Would you please make the text for learned ATLAS words red or some other color so that I can more easily see what my character knows, and what are just random compilations of letters? It feels inconsistent to do that for the main alien races but not for the ATLAS' speech. 

Overall, I'd highly recommend this game; I had loads of fun playing it. The one flaw with the game can also be a good thing: everything is procedurally generated so after the first couple of planets/freighters/buildings you've seen them all.

I'd give it 10 of 10.

Recommended NO but with a disclaimer: I'm still going to play, it's fun and it scratches an itch.

First of all, I didn't play at launch nor in the following years. I'm a fresh player, these hours I have are from the past month or so.

Secondly, I'll start with the cons.

THE UI

It's a complete mess. The inventory system is clunky, unwieldly and a goddamn frustrating experience. Sometimes it works, but most of the time, it doesn't. I like to keep a tidy inventory and so, when I quick transfer 100 Oxygen to my freighter's storage, I expect it to land in the same stack as the other 100 Oxygen there. Sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn't and it's infuriating.

Interacting with containers, terminals, NPCs is sloooooooooow. Why, oh why, do I have to wait 2-3 seconds after "cleaning" some cargo drops in order to loot the actual loot? NPCs are the worst offenders; usually, you interact four times with a lifeform: to learn a new word then to practice your language skills 3 times. Why does it have to push you out of the dialogue EACH and EVERY time you talk, then forces you to click click click click through the mindblowingly stupid dialogue?

Not to mention the incredibly intrusive "help" messages. I'VE BEEN FLYING FOR 60 HOURS, I KNOW HOW TO TAKE OFF! And no, you can't turn them off. Need help for a quest? Don't worry, we'll remind you every 2 seconds with an annoying blip on what you need to do.

Also, was it really necessary to give the suit a robotic voice? A stupid one? Really?

The story is very boring so far; it's like it was written by a 12 year old with a space fetish; instead of actually creating a "story" you get a bunch of kzzzt kzzzt - n`189718568651378 - KZZZT for "atmosphere" (which is very lazy in my opinion) and when you do get dialogue it's mumbo jumbo LSD trip influenced crap.

All these little things are....little, to be fair. But they add up and they can get frustrating.

Flying is meh. I don't have much experience with flight sims or other space flying games. Space combat is very meh: just press S, aim and shoot. Combat on the ground is extremely meh. I think they only added combat, in general, because it would be very weird if there was a completely peacefull galaxy. It feels very rushed and just thrown together in an "OH SHIT WE FORGOT COMBAT" moment.

For the moment, I'm done with the bad. On with the good!

I love the graphics and the randomness of the planets. I love the exploring, jumping from system to system not knowing what I'll find. I like the crafting, upgrading and the economy. 

I absolutely adore base building and the freighter/frigate systems. The starships are amazing and sometimes I just stand around looking at them.

Landing on a planet for the first time, looking around, scanning then getting into my exocraft to explore is the core of the game for me and it's why I keep playing.

Sure, there are missions, quests, a storyline (like I said) but meh. I spend my time taking care of my fleet, my base and exploring the universe which...is where the game really shines.

That being said, this is why I consider this game to be a mixed bag and a rollercoaster of emotions: when I get frustrated with the stupid NPCs, I can just jump into my starship and explore. Combat is annoying? Mess around with my fleet. Storyline is borderline retarded? Build a new place in an ocean of acid!

Hello Games have slowly redeemed themselves for what was, for many, a disappointing release. At this point I believe their game is worth experiencing.

When this game was released many gave a lot of flak to them, and specially Sean Murray, for not living up to expectations. What Murray shared with people in his interviews about the game was his vision, his passion for his creation. The dream was huge, a beautiful vision of an infinite universe filled with life for you to explore. I’m inclined to believe his error was sharing with us his vision and not what they could realistically achieve.

This game is mostly what you make out of it, because it is primarily a sandbox exploration game with no meaningful ending. 

Mine resources, build technology and upgrades for your suit and ship, jump to another system and repeat. Explore the planets, hunt for flora and fauna or ignore them completely.
Build a nice base and when you are done with it barely ever come back to it. Trivialize any resource and unit collection with mining bases or just grind it by yourself. Whatever you enjoy.
Other aspects of the game sadly lack enough variation to keep you in awe for long, but as I said, the vision of what they intended to build here is huge. They could keep updating this game for years to come and it would never be big enough.

The game has a handful of quests. I consider their narrative to be fairly dark, but fitting. I think that adds up to the existential dread of how small and insignificant we are compared to the universe, even to this one created for us by Hello Games.

One of the best games I've encountered in the last years. I don't want to repeat the facts mentioned in other reviews, instead I'll try to illustrate my fascination with some personal milestones and cover some bad parts afterwards:

* I found a very stylish exotic spaceship, upgraded it to the max and matched everything to its color theme.
* I found the birdlike Ewoks of the press image, I found a nice lush home planet.
* I built the first base of my dreams, maybe more to come.
* I found pillars of light, ancient portals with unknown function, I got a glimpse of the grim history of the alien races.
* I travelled to the center of the galaxy, I saw the fate of the universe.
* I completed quests and raided infested freighters with a friend.
* I searched more than an hour in the depths of the sea to scan the last rare creature of my home planet. It was a tranquil trip and finding the marine dinosaur was very satisfying.

Coming to negative aspects:

* It has bugs, I've encountered several. But in over 300 hours no really game breaking one like some other reviews described.
* It has a lot of grind, well that may actually be the core of the game. But there is always so much variety that it never feels like that. If some grindy action gets boring, well just do something else rewarding, there are always meaningful options. So much more interesting than the grind in all action RPGs so far.
* There is not enough diversification of biomes. The exploration aspect is nevertheless fascinating and I hope for updates of this area.
* The quest lines are rather short and not complex. I consider them a nice addition, yet I'm still not finished since I'm distracted too easily by other options of the game ;-)

One last positive point. All (big!) updates of the last four years were free. No DLC to buy. The game has no micropayment bullsh**, even though it has extremely obvious options for it, due to its grindiness and special ingame currency for mainly cosmetic enhancements. I'm looking forward to the next great updates, thanks to the devs!

So should you buy the game or not? After reading negative reviews, which do cover valid issues, it may be this question:

Imagine an exotic planet to explore and the option to build a great base of your own. No quest says to do so, you won't save the world by doing it. Will you explore the planet and build your base, just because you can? If yes, buy this game. Immediately. If no, read more reviews and consider whether this is really your type of game.

Talk about a comeback story. This game promised Peter Molyneux levels of gameplay and delivered none of them in it's original release. Over the course of a few years they could have taken the easy way out and just taken their money and run or charged a whole bunch of money for "DLC". None of that happened, instead they slowly brought the game to where it was supposed to be and it's fantastic.

The graphics are pretty good and colorful, if that's your thing. The gameplay is very deep and there is something for almost everyone. You can get lost for hours just plunking around exploring. Although I will say some of it gets a little repetitive or boring after too long. Once you've seen one "Oxygen Rich Plant" you've seen all the little red plants. Although I will say, I enjoy the loading screen a lot more than I have in any other game.

If you're a fan of games where you set your own pace and just want to chill out, you could do a lot worse than No Man's Sky. 

The sound and audio is great. The music soundtrack is brought to you by 65daysofstatic, a weird name but they deliver. The moments that hit you with awe are brought to an even higher level by the soundtrack. This is one of those games that you can buy the music and enjoy it, even if you hate the game.

I bought this game when it first released, played until I got to the Galactic Core, then shelved it. It was mildly fun at the time, but there wasn't much to hold my attention.
Years later when Hello Games adapted the game for VR, I'd already been into VR for a couple of years myself, and decided to play it again. I have hundreds of hours of playtime in NMS VR now, so suffice it to say that the VR option combined with all the content updates HG has released since have kept my attention. I'm pretty much all caught up on the new story content and gameplay features, but with the promise of more updates (and continuing Weekend Events), I will leave this installed on my PC. As a sandbox, the game is engaging, letting you build as much as you like. The additional story & event content help make up for what can be an otherwise shallow experience. I don't mean to knock the game, but there's not a ton of depth there. I'd love to see more complex systems and emergent AI behavior implemented, and I'd love to see more natural planetary landscape features and variety added, as well as ruined cities to explore with their own quests (the abandoned frigates are a good start). Not to knock HG's efforts, there's just nowhere to go but up in terms of potential content. I've seen hints of some really interesting story elements coming down the pike. What's there now does finally feel like it's worth the $60 price, though if you can get the game on sale, go for it. Adapting the game to VR alone though--to me at least--totally makes this game a must-have for anyone else looking for quality VR titles. There are still a few bugs and quirks to work out in that regard, but nothing horrible, and the modding community fixes a lot (HG is not much different from BethSoft in that regard, but also like Beth, their game offers VR players a LOT of potential playtime for their money).

Granted, when the game first came out, for $60 it was 110% hot garbage.

Like many, I started playing NMS several years after it was released, specifically after the BEYOND update.  I just wanted to explore the vastness of space, and found games like Elite: Dangerous to be more complicated than I wanted to deal with.

NMS fit the bill.  Settle down with a drink and chill as you  warp around space.  Sure, at first you have to put some effort in to get a good ship and to get it upgraded, then I just concentrated on warping to the galaxy center one hop at a time.  Then doing it again.  And again.  

It was fun, saw some cool things, but after a hundred hours or so, you realize you've pretty much seen every type of system and planet there is.  Sure, I could keep warping to find the perfect Earth-like planet with nice green grass, blue waters, and little sentinel activity, but then what?  

I could build a base, but they don't really serve a purpose.  I could get a bunch of credits, but they have limited use too.

So I'll walk away from the game feeling I got my money's worth and that the game scratched an itch I had at the time.  I know there are other additions with being underwater and exo-suits, but again, it seems like it would be a grind to get those and upgrade them, and then no real point to using them.

entry 23 // day 34 // as i'm leaving the abandonned ship behind, I cannot help but feel sorry for its poor crew. Those guys were never meant to be left in space, they didn't sign for that. they were lied to, cheated on. I've salvaged a couple entries from the diary of the captain... and I wonder. Would I have acted different ? If this infestation was to be found aboard the H99 Ryuko, what would I do ? My crew, my family, the loyal bunch I've sent all around the galaxy for sometimes dangerous missions, well aware of the risks, excited by the rewards... Never had I before considered their lives, their friends, families, those Geks waiting for them somewhere while they were chasing some maniac's dream, for him, without him. At least the harvest was bountyful : a couple upgrades for my ship, some salvaged tech, some sodium... But I understand there's a price to pay : the faces of those who lost their fight against a rigged game that never left them a chance to win, inhabiting my dreams, haunting my days. I want to leave this behind me. I want to let them rest in peace. Those upgrades... they burn my hands. I need to get rid of them. I need to throw them away, throw them to drift endlessly in space, floating mausoleums in the void, left there for anyone to find, anyone to weep over. I open the hatch, grab whatever my fingers touch, and send it all hurling in the dark. I'll go back to my base, grab a drink with my old friends, try to shush my consciousness. Flying trivialities. 
My scanner just beeped. It has completed its task and the coordinates of a hidden facility on the surface of a planet nearby popped onto my screen. I'm gonna check that out, real quick. 

I'll rest when I'm dead.

They kept working on it and now it has a ton of content! I greatly recommend, I understand the launch and lying were a huge turn off. But give these guys credit, they didn't just take the money and run. They stood behind their product and are continuing to push huge updates.

The planets are looking really good and filled with great biomes, plant life, oceans, and wildlife. But I feel they could be doing a lot more on the planets, like focusing on the missions and make them a bit more exciting or maybe give them a quest line to some treasure or something.

The fact that you can go from land to space is amazing, I feel it should take about as long to get into space as it does to land on the planet though, but other than that, they nailed the surreal feeling of being in space. I would totally do a VR for it if I owned one. 

The travelling in space is fun when jumping from planet to planet, or solar system, and you get to discover new biome planets, which there are a huge variety of. Every planet I go to, nothing looks the same, nothing is rendered the same. The fauna and visuals are gorgeous. Seeing other planets setting like the sun, its breathtaking when you take it all in. They have rainbows, weather particular to the planet which adds more to the survival aspect, and a huge variety of wildlife.

If you are going to get this game, wait for a sale of course, I personally will give this game a 8/10 due to everything I have mentioned. I for sure have missed a lot in this review, mostly because I am lazy, but I can see myself playing this for a long time, especially trying out the new big updates they push that just adds more and more to the game. 

Multiplayer sucks doe, hope they figure this one out.

Reviews.126751:
This game's redemption arc since its failure in 2016 exceeds even that of Zuko from Avatar: The Last Airbender. If you're reading this and weren't there to see it happen, this game was hyped up a *lot* back when it was about to come out, and the devs made a bunch of promises they failed to deliver on. They promised crashed freighters, portals, large space battles, sand planets, water worlds, and a whole lot more, and none of that was there at launch. All of those features were later added.

There are some things that were promised that haven't been added yet, such as the ability to land on asteroids. But Hello Games made up for that by adding a ton of cool features they never promised. Now, you can build bases, drive vehicles, ride on animals, find sunken wrecks and tech planets, farm, customize your character, own multiple ships, and a whole lot more. There's even a VR mode.

If what you're looking for is a cool space exploration game, this is exactly that. No Man's Sky won't disappoint you. It has the perfect combination of freedom to do what you'd like to and restrictions on getting what you want to keep you pulled in, warping from system to system, exploring, fighting, and trading in a procedurally generated universe.

If you are into exploring, building, survival, and shooting things then this game is going to be worth the money you spend.

Exploring
I can literally spend a couple days exploring one planet if I was to explore every bit of it. That is just one planet and there can be multiples in a system. Then you got vasts amounts of systems (vast enough it is lottery odds to see another player.)

Building
While the piece choices are somewhat limited the places you can build are not. Beach, mountaintop, underground, etc if you find the spot you can build there.

Survival
On normal the survival mechanics are kinda on the easy side. However you have the survival mode which limits how much of a stack you can carry, the conditions are more severe on a planets, and then you go more hostiles running around. If that still aint enough you have a permanent death option.

Shooting things
Combat has a minor role in the game. You can however choose to engage in it or choose to avoid it. You got everything from space pirates, Sentinnels who attack when they find someone plundering resources to wandering critter looking for lunch.

So if you are one of those people who values their money spent to time played ratios then this is one of those games you are going to spend a lot of time playing.

Reviews.126773:
K so a little late to this party and I have far too many hours into this game at this point now. 

I both Hate and Love No Man's Sky. I love it because it's amazing and so addictive, but I hate it because it is\was so close to an absolute masterpiece. To preface this, I didn't play at launch and I didn't pay any attention to the hype or drama. I simply picked up the game with my wife and started playing one day.

The Good:
- The game is simply beautiful. From planets, to animals, and everything in between it's awe inspiring. When you hop into VR and enjoy the view from your base the only game that has rivaled the visuals is super modded Skyrim.

- Still not 100% sure how they manage it, but the planetary mechanics are incredible. More planets and solar systems then you could ever come close to visiting. The game does a wonderful job of making you few tiny and insignificant (in a good way).
- Multiplayer interaction is largely smooth and enjoyable. For a game of it's scale the drop in mechanics are very clean.
- Base and freighter building is amazingly addictive. The options allow you to create works of art and building fun homes around the galaxy just happily eats up hours.

The Bad:
- The game is an adventurer's dream, but after about 50-60 hours you quickly feel all the planet types get "samey". The colors and vegetation vary slightly, but in general a cold planet looks like other cold planets, hot like hot, etc. There wasn’t enough variation in assets to make things feel unique. Even animal life boils down the typical variants.

- Minecraft like Builders will love making bases, but bugs in terrain cause your work to be buried sometimes and limitations on part count means you have to be conservative in the long run. Additionally cooperative building is a huge thing for this community, but the multiplayer mechanics only stretch so far and bases distances from each other can be an issue.

- Completionist have a TON of checkboxes to fill with languages to learn, upgrades to flesh out, reputation to gain, and every dailies if you want to get all the things. However, the devs have added extremely watered down mechanics over the years that trivialize these experiences. There is even duping bugs, crafting loopholes, and economy issues the devs seem to either not care about or don’t know how to fix. Upgrading your suit slots for example went from a task of finding and repairing upgrades found on planets, to simply just visiting a new space station and paying a nominal fee.

- Multiplayer missions are available and even cross platform with all your friends! However, the missions are extremely simplistic and often easier to do on your own. Especially when an unexpected crash can cause your teammate to lose the mission and reward. 

Now, all this said, this game teeters on the precipice of being an all time greatest like I said. Unfortunately, it’ll likely never get there. If there were to be a #2 it could attain this level with better focus from the dev team. Being 240+ hours into the game as of writing this, I HIGHLY recommend picking up the game, on discount. The level of bugs, simplified mechanics, and the likelihood of never quite being would it could have been do not warrant the retail tag.

Any time I want to just distract myself, NMS is there. The core of the game, to me, is simple exploration. Searching for every new animal species on a planet will take days. Expanding my knowledge of one of the 3 languages is on-going & seemingly never ending. In the recent expansion, there are now "space wrecks" to (rarely) find & explore, with their own mini stories, too.

Overall, I think it's a good game that got a lot of hate & (still) has a little bit too high of a price tag. Maybe wait for it to be $30-$40 on sale.

I have had this game for a couple years. I remember the days of the hot mess it was. The game on release, was a hot pile of messy dog poo you stepped in walking through the park near some trees while you were checking out the hot girl across the way and then walked through a spider web cause you weren't watching where you were going and started swinging at seeming nothingness as she just so happened to look up and see you. Yeah , it was that.

Since the game's release there have been 12 patches applied to the game. Now while not all of these patches were major, there are some that have added enough content and helped the game become playable versus it's previous incarnations. 

There are current reviews that will tell you the game is bad. This is not the case. The game in it's current form is playable and entertaining. The issue with current reviews is, they are basing it across their entire interaction with the game and still holding to the original game state. 

If the game was released today as it is, current form, people would still find issues with it as they always do, but it wouldn't be the hateful drivel you see posted. 

My experience in the game, 124ish hours played in the game. Unfinished. No living ship. No freighter. I haven't even scratched the surface of the game. The issue?  45 or so hours of that 124 were played over the time span of two or so years. I have put in the rest of the time over the last two to three weeks.  

- GAME TECHNICAL-
The game is not technically a survival game, but more of search and seek. There aren't that many things that challenge your mortality that you can't get away from if needed. 
-ENGINE TECHNICAL-
There are still some fluctuations with the game as far as graphics and ram management. The classic stutter that has always been there when you turn too fast for the processing to happen. 

The game has captured my attention and finally has become something playable and entertaining. Would I purchase in at the full price of 60.oo USD? Nope... Not EVER. But then again, I won't buy any game at that price. I would support the devs in earnest though, I just wouldn't pay full price on anything. If you can find it cheaper, do so.

PROS:

No Man's Sky is an amazing game with an incredible story, making you question almost everything you think of as 'real'.(Don't play if you are having mental issues! The game is a bit nihilistic.) The worlds are beautiful and strange, and there are literally 18 quintillion planets to explore.

The story is very deep, and can be very depressing at times. No spoilers, but some of the choices made later in the story are really thought opening, and your choices are irreversable and will stick with you throughout the game.

From what I've heard, No Man's sky can be switched to VR without any setup, but I have yet to try this for myself.

CONS:

While No Man's Sky is an emotional trip, its gameplay is rather lacking at the moment. The only enemies in the game are called 'sientels' and attack you whenever you loot something valuable. They come in the shapes of floaty dude, dog dude, and giant dude. Once you know how to deal with them, there isn't much of a reason to max out your gun.

In space, the only thing to fight is other spaceships like you, be gek, korvax, vykeen, or sientel. Same issues as planetary combat.

There really isn't much to do after the game is completed. While the planets are beautiful, they lack in entertaining things to do. There isn't anything in the game that is particuarly rare to find (asides from ships and guns, more on that later) which means there isn't really a reason to dig down. Even if you wanted to, you aren't allowed to dig more than a couple feet under. That kicks out underground bases, cave exploration, grinding, and fighting as discussed earlier. 

When it comes to rarity, Ships and Guns go overboard. While not really needed, Grinding for S-Rank guns, ships, and frigates are the closest you will get to accomplishing something big in the game. Even then, you can just look up seeds for S-rank guns and ships, and you can just save scum for an S-Rank Frigate. It is also very hard to get one of them legit. The only S rank I have ever found on my own was a S-class carrier, due to how many can spawn at a single place. For guns, you would have to go planet to planet, solar system to solar system for at least a couple hours to find something decent.

I really just wish there was something to accomplish after completing the game. It doesn't have much replayability, and it doesn't have much to do after you've completed the game. Playing it again is like watching a horror movie the second time; There isn't anything new to find, and everything that got you the time before sort of just... flops.


CONCLUSION:
I wouldn't say that No Man's Sky is bad. I really enjoyed the game. I just wish that there was more to do.

I got 65 hours out of it, and payed about 40$, so the game costed about $0.62 per hour I spent on it. They were fairly enjoyable, but only 5-10 hours were spent playing the game after I had completed it.

If your looking for something more cost effective, I would just get minecraft or terraria. They got a bit more replayability, a bit to do after completing the game, and a bit more creative liberty. It makes me sound like a kid, but its true.

I'm giving this game a 5/10. 
It's not particularly good, but not particularly bad either. 

In fact, it is a hodge-podge of stuff, and you can spend some time with each aspect of it.
The developers have added all sorts of features, but each of these features is kind of ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

Here are the things that prevent me from considering it a good game:
 - This is supposedly a space game. Like, you can fly a starship, but doing so is not great. In space you can fly to planets, shoot at asteroids and occasionally some pirates will turn up. Mining asteroids gets boring really quickly, and the pirates are all laughably easy to beat, so that isn't interesting after the first few times either. In the end, your starhip is just a bus that gets you to other places and a storage container for some extra inventory items.

 - The planets are terrible. Bland, undifferentiated, boring. As places, the planets make no sense. Why are the buildings dotted about randomly instead of forming settlements? Why does every planet have the same rolling hills, instead of plains or sharp mountains? Why is there no variation in terrain on a single planet? Where are the rivers and waterways on planets tha have rain? Why are there re-entry burn effects on "airless" planets? Why is there no climate difference between the polar and equatorial regions? Why are there cargo crates all over the surface of absolutely every planet? etc, etc.

 - The story is hot garbage. What's the point of all that stuff with travellers and anomalies???

 - There is no map. You're basically lost all the time. I had to use my starship and search from the air to find the location of a mineral extractor I had set up outside my base...
At the very least, I wanted the ability to set persistent NAMED custom markers. The beacons in the game are simply not good enough.

 - Crashes. There were several. I got crashes to desktop and crashes to boot. There were also lockups where the game just stopped and had to be killed with task manager. It's not unusable, but I did seem to get a problem in just about every gaming session. Frequent saving is definitely a good idea.

Conclusion
I have played for about 50 hours (I have no idea how steam got it's number - did it continue counting after a crash?) and that is probably the outermost limit the game is good for. I regret not stopping a few days ago.
Still, this is enough that there is no doubt I got fair value from the game.

The game has absolutely come leaps and bounds from what it was at launch, which even wasn't that bad of an initial product to begin with. The amount of interesting content that the HG team has put in and the amount of work ethic they've put towards the game is really admirable and I have a lot of respect for them in that regards. 

Positives: 

- The games atmosphere is incredible (granted the whole game is literally atmosphere sometimes but no pun intended) 

- The narrative is really enthralling and is written in such a way that you have to apply some of your own imagination to get the gist of what is being told to you. 

- The amount of customization is pretty expansive for all you base builders out there. 

- I'm constantly taking photos, no matter how long I play there's always something I see that's just too pretty to not capture it somehow. Visually fantastic game (minus some of the fauna, you know the one)

Like any game though there are some flaws:

If you're reading this, you probably already know this -- but No Man's Sky is good now. Really, really good. On launch, it didn't meet the immense hype that had been built up for this game. But in the years since its initial release, the devs have clearly put a tremendous amount of work into this game, and it now somehow actually lives up to the initial hype. If you haven't played it, it is very, very good -- and entirely worth your time and money.

As someone who bought this for full price in the first week, I would have initially given it a 7/10. It wasn't a bad game, but it felt unfinished -- the worlds felt a bit empty, the progression system felt patchy, and the overall story felt too minimalistic. I enjoyed it -- I came close to beating it, even -- but it gave me the same vibes as Spore.

Having just now picked it up again for the first time in four years, it feels like a true 10/10. The worlds feel so much fuller, with exotic plants and fauna, overlapping incentives, and clear goals to complete on each planet by way of the new (to me) questing system. I've started a new character, and the game guides you along, easing you in to all of the new features over what's (so far) been a 12ish hour experience. I'm that far in, and I'm still finding new gameplay mechanics -- which isn't to say that it feels like a tutorial, just a truly grand adventure.

To sum up: if you like the idea of building a base from scratch (think Minecraft), flying from that base into fast-paced space combat (think Starfox 64), parking your spaceship into a freighter (think EVE Online), and then piloting that freighter into the center of the galaxy (no point of comparison), this is the game for you. It combines exploration, survival, base building, space combat, and a beautiful, procedurally generated universe into a truly unique experience. And the dev team deserves so much more praise than they've been given for updating this game for four years straight in order to live up to the initial hype.

Buy it today!

No Man's Sky is a wonderful, open-world game which gives you freedom to fly around in a plethora of space ships. You can do almost anything; from fighting hostile aliens, to raiding planetary factories - the choice really is up to the player.

That being said...

Although No Mans Sky gives you lots of freedom to fly around the galaxy, travelling from planet to planet, the vast universe feels...well...empty!

90% of the content in the games is bound to the player flying from star system to star system, exploring the same planets, completing the same challenges and tasks. This is a great game, and I love it, but the game really stunts itself, by not giving the player enough freedom!

Instead, you just find yourself in ground hog day, doing the same tasks just to get credits. Frankly - Its Boring!

Though No Mans Sky does a lot, it doesn't do enough.

Everything about it just feels... unconnected. It attempts to do a lot, but many of the core mechanics are so flawed and awkward. Take flying for example. Its meant to feel good, soaring through space, travelling down to planets. But actually, it feels horrible! There is some algorithm that's meant to stop you from crashing, but all it does, is cause crashes! 

As a summary:

I would definitely rate buying this game on sale, rather than at the full £40.
It is definitely a unique experience, but at its current state, is just a little bit lacking!

Not worth a review. I played nearly 1000 hours only to stumble again and again on the small things, inconveniences, annoyances and finally bugs. I will probably play some more, but today, as I finally thought 'I HAVE to play', not that 'I WANT to play', I decided to write few words about my experiences. I have no VR and play with no mods whatsoever, so read with that in mind. I want to stress that fact because apparently mods can make one's live easier, but hey, this is a review of the game and a picture of the dev studio, not the community.

Aside from bugs, one has to constantly learn what doesn't work. You'd think you can put your crap into a box and return to get it, only to find that the box is there but it's contents were lost, this kind of thing. That you discover a place only to find it later being 'unknown building'. It's tiring after a time, I'm surprised for how long I put up with it. I guess there was something else I wanted to do that made me play and play still. Finally there's nothing more I want to do and I wish no one else has to pay for a trip to this masochistic adventure. Unless they like that sort of thing, whatever.

Setting aside all the annoyances, there comes the story. It is a mixture of technology, myths, mysticism and magic. Many times I felt it's on the level of a low-grade japanese light novel or web manga. Fortunately one can just click through and ignore it. I tried to play once ignoring the story completely from the start (i.e. not going to do what the initial quest was about, repairing the crashed ship and all that) but the story adjusted to my actions and again forced itself on me when I acquired another starship, so yeah, wasted some hours for no reason.

Finally there are bugs and they are long standing. Surprising is the fact that devs release content updates but are not willing to fix bugs. Unwilling? or maybe Unable? both ways is bad anyway. I reported myself 25 bugs during 4 months I played and out of that fixed were 2 (two). Things like game exiting in certain situations or plain hang for no reasons are still there, so be warned. Some don't encounter them, some do more than others, especially AMD Radeon owners (like me).

So that's it. I had my intermittent times of fun, I mostly fought to do things the way I want but was bitten by the game, got hyped then disappointed, you know, the standard... or is it?

A few forewords; My playtime is inflated from leaving the game open for timed frigate missions while asleep.
[h1]TL;DR - [/h1] The amount of enjoyment you'll get out of this game is about as much as you're willing to give it. Which is about as roundabout as pretending you're a dog who needs someone to tell you you're a good boy. This game is a surrogate stationary hand that you can rub your own head against and supply your own imagination and dopamine. In other words; there’s enough art assets and structure here for you to have a little fun on the first few runs essentially boiling down to that Nightmare Before Christmas song; "What's this?! What's this?!". It's a box. A very big box but very sparse box. It's got some playtime for the newness. Don't bother full price. Strong chance that you'll want to regret it afterwords but see your play hours and think it was at least worth it on the time to money spent ratio. 

  Before we get started, I have to admit something to anyone bothering to read this; I'm not entirely sure if I'm here just to winge or rage against all of the possitive sentiment going about the game,  actually critique the game, or try to persuade someone to buy this or not. I had been wanting to write a review for ages but it was always after leaving the game feeling slighted and I just don't think that vitriol is any good reason to bash anything, so I had to take time to cool off. But every time I came back to the game it always ended the same way and I became sure I had a point to make beyond just "I did not like my time spent." So, this will more or less devolve in to a personal account and selfish review. As I feel like I need to shed my burning thoughts on my "want to like/hate" relationship with this game. 
And, while I don't want to come off as openly hostile to readers, I'm more than well aware of the ... eh, general lack of decorum and critical thinking of steam's typical comment sections; rabid fans going full apologist/death to the devs for not fulfilling their expectations.  So I'm not gunna bother with allowing comments here. I know what I'll get. 

   I did not start at the famous launch of this game. Heard about it from sparse articles around, and bought in for curiosity somewhere near ... Atlas Rises I think? The game has ... rearranged rather than evolved a lot since then. Far less content but no matter how much or little content that is in the game I feel like the same core gameplay loops occurred anyways. It becomes stupidly repetitive due to the modular nature. This isn't really something I can rightfully fault the game for since, well, how does one plan to realistically have billions of iterations of something? I may not like it, but I can forgive it. It's just the nature of the style of this game. 

   I feel the immediate need to set that sentiment apart from base apologism; I feel that was the intention integral to the game as a whole. It’s not a misgiving, misstep, or fault on the creators that I feel I need to lie to myself about being okay with to avoid the whole sunk cost fallacy or to just avoid negativity in general. Which, does rather sum up this whole game to me; the base formula being hypothetically brilliant, endless, and an amazing concept. But like all iterations of an ideal, it is limited to its means available. I can’t rightly go around faulting this game for not being the very best thing I could have ever seen. I feel I can only rightly fault something for not being the best iteration of itself it could be. 

   Which brings us to something I'd call an inherently fatal flaw in the technology, not entirely the idea. But this does depend on where one personally draws the line. All the planets .... have the same sort of feel to them. The hills are very gradual, I've never found any significant unique formations like ice caps or mountains or things of that nature. Color palletes are novel at first, Planet A is blue, Planet B is green. They're both so alike topographically that I wouldn't notice. Everything in the game ends up giving you the feeling of a placeholder. A cardboard cut out. I feel this way about most forms of substance in the game; ships, bases, and every bit of new content released. 

   To which, I hear some fruitlessly typing in argument; "But that’s all video games, they're just fake approximations of form and substance. Your argument is invalid. Nerd." To which I'd say, [b]yes![/b] You get the fundamentals of art! [i]Not entirely why humans even bother making art; not as a replacement or a surrogate, but something new. Something to be shared as an experience.[/i] But, go back to invalidating everything you see just because you can make a roundabout argument based on the first thing that pops in your head because you weren't hugged enough. Go on, you're doing god's work, Timmy!

   I’ll take an aside to this aside and apologize if you are someone who does regularly attempt to make rational arguments in good faith. I would love to say you know who you are, but the types who do make intelligent arguments in good faith and those who don't and just spew random vitriol, don't always know which they are. For better or worse, unfortunately.

   Either way back to the issue at hand; this philosophical thought that, if everything in a video game is just a proxy; why bother or care at all? I believe that falls under reductio ad absurdum. As rather than a Neitzche-ian "Nothing has meaning" I feel it’s more like "Anything can have meaning in a world devoid of any barrier to meaning." If nothing HAS to have meaning; that means it’s free to do what it wants. It could have any meaning. 

    And No Man's Sky feels like it takes that philosophy to the deepest part of its heart. At which point, it's where we run in to that issue of art being subjective. Someone uninspired could make a game out of nothing but ms-paint squares with names and a few buttons, charge a whole bunch of money, and still get paid from various factors leading to purchases. Someone more inspired could make a bit more depth to the game with a better sense of taste, style, effort, and attitude. It may not be the brush strokes on the canvas, but it’s the difference in a painting that gives you a sense of mastery and beauty versus one that feels uninspired or disengaging. 

   So with that argument out of the way, I can put most of my distaste for the game down as being defeated rationally and logically. What I can’t put down is my distaste for NMS’s own iteration of the formula; I feel like it’s uninspired, bland, and almost intentionally made to the halfway level of “placeholder”. The whole game is a placeholder for an adventure. A very expensive D&D set. And their VR port just … shouldn’t have happened. That too, is a placeholder.  No room scale, very little interactions, and is just another way to see cardboard cutouts. Awesome at first, but maddening when you have to use a mod to disable all of the godawful design decisions made on that entire front. It adds nothing and at launch was a travesty with pop ups always in your face and crushed expectations.  I have many interaction issues using index but I’m not certain if that’s index specific (Can’t ever point to the right thing I want, constantly accidentally activate things off screen when I’m obviously pointing at something in front of me.) 

 So with that rant out of the way, I have finally vented. NMS is not a game lacking in effort or scale. It is lacking in inspiration. It’s an indie title that provides a cool iteration on a novel concept and ends up as a placeholder. I don’t think it shouldn’t have been made, I think it shouldn’t have had to spend years apologizing, and I don’t think it’s ever going to be a good “game” in my eyes. I struggle to call it even a game. I don’t think it deserves half the praise it gets. It’s an indie title that served a niche. And only got popular from controversy. It’s not a success story. It’s a story. A placeholder for a better iteration.

After a devastation launch, a lot of word that the game was improved went around. Many of the features promised were implemented, and more. With the trust of a friend, I bought the game, and then forced my friends to play it after I was in awe of how the game came to be.

The procedural generation is out of this world--you don't need me to explain it. However, the content seems to loop. Although there are still interesting things to find after 100 hours into the game, it eventually falters into an endless cycle of predictable, detectable patterns that sour the game and dull it a lot.

I'm not a fan of the campaign nor the story, provided that stories in games are important to me. There are upgrades and weapons, but nothing much to shoot at or fight; the combat in the game is severely lacking in depth. When I go out to earn new weapons or upgrades, I want greater challenges to use them on, but there aren't anything besides some sentinels that appear the same way and some pirates. 

Instead of new content and features, I'd prefer if Hello Games really perfected the fundamentals a lot more. The animals and creatures don't behave differently, they have no relation to their habitat or environment, their behavior is all the same all across the board. The quests and sidequests leave something to be desired, and the exocrafts are almost redundant, as they don't really add much to the game because there is almost nothing to use them on. 

The economic system is incredibly broken. The problem with any game when it comes to economy is that, a massively open world and multiplayer game like this would benefit immensely from a player-regulated economy, yet we have NPC's that have unlimited money, buy anything and everything at a fixed price at any time, no real demand, no supply, units seem incredibly inflated and insanely easy to get, pricing of ships and stuff are incredibly cheap, and finding rare items become a chore of chance rather than something you go out and earn. 

The derelict freighters are a perfect example of something that I don't want... YET. It's a great idea, but the game seems to lack in fundamentals and it keeps adding new features but nothing to use them on. The derelict freighters take a page from Dead Space, but not enough; the aliens aren't creepy or horrifying, they're actually adorable, which is the opposite of what it should've been. There's no big boss, there's no real mystery, the logs tell not show, the procedural room generations become endless, predictable loops. You really start to see a pattern here.

This game is beautiful, but it has faults. Its foundations and fundamentals need to be perfect, where then, each new feature will compound on top of the already great game it could be, but these new features aren't multiplying the fun.

Good things:

You can (eventually) fly anywhere. Discover any number of stars and planets, full of life, treasure, and opportunity. 
Your ships, ground vehicles, bases, tools, and suit can all be modified and upgraded in many ways.
You can command your own fleet of ships, including your massive freighter. 
Flying in VR is pretty cool.
Dogfighting works pretty well, and is enjoyable.
The visuals are amazing...mostly.
Seemingly endless creatures which can be cataloged and tamed.
Some realism in how you acquire languages.

Bad things:

Bugs. So many bugs. Not the crawly kind.

The story is a disconnected mess that makes little or no sense, and defeats almost all interest in following it. Even when you do find out some of the secrets to your existence, it's not cool or fun enough to want to turn the page. Some of the 'discoveries' are impressive, but I would rather know who and what I am at the beginning; that way I might feel more grounded . Instead you are literally an 'iteration' with a vague purpose and no identity. Have you ever wanted to actually BE a simulation? Yeah, me neither.

The alien races look fairly cool and have different personalities, but are unified in being brightly colored and child-like. It's a bit like walking around an elementary-school playground, but without the bullies, sense of competition, or the sharp-edged cruelty of a random kick-ball to the face. They live in a universe full of pirates, and deadly sentinels, but they act like friendly cartoon characters at all times. They never feel like they have any kind of agenda or loyalties, fears, or cares. They are just friendly automatons having a really nice day. Great for a vacation maybe, not for a space adventure.

Wasn't really sure what to expect when I picked it up after the Desolation update.

But my expectations were blown away regardless.

It's got base building, ship scrapping, weapon upgrading, exocraft racing, deep sea exploration, cook your own cuisine, like 5 different storylines, stock prices and trading, and like a hundred other things. I had no idea! And each section of the game feels polished to some degree, like someone put some real love into crafting it.

Some of my favorite experiences thus far:

-Stumbling upon a derelict space station, devoid of intelligible life, and being chased my the sentinel ships that spewed forth from it. Decided to fight back with the aid of my friends, until they sent in a flippin capitol ship to take us out. It was like a laser light show.
-Just got my submersible exocraft geared up and went diving around. Found a massive underwater cave network, brimming with life and color. Eventually stumbled upon a really decent ship that had crashed and sank to the bottom, and salvaged it from the murky depths.
-Did the weekly Nexus mission with my friends. I had the foresight to bring materials for an exocraft bay. We spent hours just ripping around a planet in our Roamers, doing mad jumps and running over the wildlife.
-I've built a massive oceanside base on top of the water, and have spent a good portion of time setting up that tiki party vibe that I get to enjoy every time I fly in from space.

The game today is a phenomenal experience, and I am looking forward to playing it for a long while to come.

[h1]Serious Question to the Devs[/h1]
How the hell did you guys manage to deal with all the backlash and hate when this game first came out. Yes it obviously wasn't ready for the public but how did you guys have the tolerance and dedication to keep on pushing to make this game what it is now. I think you guys would make the world's best anger management therapists because you had the whole world against you and you managed to not give up and believe in the dream for this game. As a result, you have changed everyone's minds and earned your respect and love that you clearly deserve. Please tell us how you guys managed to deal with the stress that I doubt anyone else could have handled.

[h1]Pros[/h1]

[b] Tons of stuff to do [/b]
Each time you play, it feels like you are going on a different adventure. You tell yourself you should get done one thing today like mining copper but then you are like "Oh there's a nearby outpost, I might as well check it out while I'm close". Then it reveals something important, then you go and check that out, and before you know it you are now on the other side of the planet trying to learn language and realize you should try to get that copper next time you play.

[b] Satisfying Rewards [/b]
Compared to other grind games, this game has extremely satisfying rewards with new toys that are amazing to use such as frigates and vehicles and new ships to use.

[b] Multiplayer [/b]
Although the multiplayer in my opinion isn't as good as something like Minecraft because it's harder to build a base and get started together, there definitely are some amazing interactions you can get with your friends. Such as when someone in VR can kill you in 2 punches or you are mining underground and the screen starts shaking so you think there's an earthquake, only to realize your friend is shooting at you from space and about to crash into you.

[b] Game is beautiful [/b]
You can already see from the trailers but when you start the game, my god does the game look amazing. A big reason why you want to explore is just to see how beautiful this game is.

[h1]Cons[/h1]

[b] Lots of Grinding [/b]
For some you may not mind the grind but for others this issue could be the thing that drives you away from enjoying this game. Yeah, there is tons of stuff to collect to make progress but the payoff is worth it.

[b] Low variety on planets [/b]
Although there is lots of stuff to do on the planets, there aren't many differences between the planets. Sure some resources are only available on specific planets but a lot of stuff and the same fauna are pretty much on every planet. The fauna only look slightly different and they all function the same. The dangerous plants and creatures can be found on most of the planets with little to no differences in behavior or appearances.

[b] Glitches [/b]
If you look on the game's subreddit, you can see all the crazy glitches people have experienced and they are so funny like NPC's being sideways, getting launched out of your ship, or being able to flip your ship while going through hyperspace but some of these can be game breaking from falling through the ground to terrain disappearing when using the terrain tool and so on.

[b] Long Loading Screens [/b]
In the game's defense there is a lot to load but man does it take a while. From 2 minutes to when you start your profile to about 30 seconds when you go through a teleporter, it just gets really annoying. Look I know the starting loading screen for when you launch the profile is really cool as you go by the stars but I'd rather just have a black screen if it means I can start the game faster.

[b] Bad Tutorial [/b]
When you first start the game, it's hard to figure out what you are supposed to do and how the game works. Sure the beauty of this game is discovering everything on your own and being surprised but the problem is that the game becomes very confusing for those who just started the game. It's usually better to have an experienced friend guide you through the start of the game before they let you do your own thing once you get comfortable with how the game works.

[b] Very Slow Early Game [/b]
For some this is not an issue at all but for others, the game's slow start may prevent you from seeing what makes this game so great. It's one of those games like Runescape or Animal Crossing where you start with nothing but with a lot of dedication, you get to admire all your hard work.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
My recommendation for this game depends on what kind of games you enjoy. If you don't like doing lots of grinding, then you won't like this game because you will feel like you are only doing the same few things over and over again. However, if you really like the games like Stardew Valley, Animal Crossing, Runescape, and Minecraft where you basically start with nothing and many weeks/months later of dedication you have an amazing farm/island/character/home base or whatever, then yeah go ahead and get this game because my god there is so much to do and before you know it, you basically have a galactic empire. I admit I'm not really a fan of those kinds of games and yet I have become addicted to this game.

It all feels unfinished. Many parts of the game are repetitive. The combat is simple and you are never in danger.

The quests are all simple. I got tired of them quickly. The main story dialogue is vague mumbo jumbo. Quests often contain incorrect instructions and many quests don't work unless you manually select it in the quest list.

There are many imbalanced or broken ways to make far too much money. It all feels like the designers didn't test things or are throwing loot at players to apologize for the games weaknesses. I stumbled across these techniques in normal game play, not looking for them. Here are a few.

1 - You can refine materials in a few steps to quickly double the amount, which violates both conservation of mass and good game design. This makes money at a very fast rate by just sitting at your base loading refiners. 

2 - Trading between solar systems makes millions of credits. You just do some quick travel and are not in any danger. The decisions of where to go and what to buy follow a simple pattern.

3 - There are cartographer maps that reveal crashed ships. The ships can be sold for scrap for millions of credits. It's way too much reward for an easy activity. 

The planets look pretty good but each one is uniform across its surface. After you look around your first landing spot you know exactly how the whole planet looks. The planets also don't look very different from each other. After you've seen the main styles of planet, the rest of the universe feels very repetitive.

The hand crafted 3-D models are all very attractive, including plants, animals, and minerals, but they don't have interesting behavior. They are evenly and densely sprinkled across the planet, so you don't need to explore much to see all the art on each planet.
