As you're likely aware, this game is huge. There are definitely some problems with the game but nothing that makes it unplayable. The most unpleasant thing in the game is trying to complete the achievement for discovering all of the fauna (animals) on a planet. I won't go too far into why it's frustrating, but just know that sometimes you can spend 8 hrs on a planet and not find the last thing you're looking for even if you're looking in the right places. 

The game also has some performance issues, specifically if you're still using Windows 7. There's a security protocol you'll need to download in order to see the Nexus Missions that award Quicksilver. Without the update you can't see them - fortunately there's a post that provides a link to what you need and it's a 30-second fix. The game also has difficulty being captured by OBS if you're a streamer. In order to capture it you'll need to be absolutely positive that you run OBS as administrator or it WILL NOT work. 

IF USING WINDOWS 7 READ THIS STEAM POST AND INSTALL THE "EASY FIX": https://steamcommunity.com/app/275850/discussions/0/2823131412464611138/

The normal difficulty of the game is really easy. After you get a few upgrades for your exosuit environmental protection there's really no reason you should ever die on that difficulty.

Survival on the other hand offers a SIGNIFICANT increase in difficulty. It is not uncommon to die in the first 10 mins of that mode and have to restart (if playing permadeath) because starting out is just incredibly unforgiving. Every decision you make about your movement can end your life which can result in having to start over completely (permadeath) or losing your entire inventory / starship etc. on Survival mode. Needless to say this adds a lot of replay value and satisfaction to the game. One of the most annoying things about it is how much fall damage there is... I really wish they'd at least decrease that, as that's one of the EASIEST AND WORST ways to die. So incredibly frustrating.

The game is almost too large for its own good, but it has had SIGNIFICANT amounts of updates to allow you to play with your friends whenever you want and to do missions with the community. If you're itching for some multiplayer action it's only a warp away now.

Load times are pretty long so you'll definitely want this on your SSD drive.

Overall I've had so much fun with this game... I'm about 40 hrs into my normal playthrough and wrapping up my journey milestones for the achievements then I am going to play on only Survival and Permadeath after that. One permadeath run for the achievement and then the rest of my time on the game will be on Survival.

I think it's important that there be SOME significant consequences for dying, and I think that the thrill of fighting for your life is completely lost on normal difficulty after you get rolling. There's not really much of any consequences to dying on normal either. Some will argue that Normal should be called Survival and Survival should be called Nightmare but I think those people are just uneducated, tbh.

Another complaint about the game would be that the planet environments from the layouts to the flora/fauna all become very familiar even when swapping between planets which is obviously not realistic at all. Despite that, the world is huge and vast, and there's no reason to feel as if you need to explore it all because you never will. Ever. There is more to explore in this game than could be done in literally hundreds of millions of years. Not sure what the exact figure is but you can google it. It's insane.

The game has a large variety of exocraft for you to test out and explore planets with. There's lots of base building you can do, portable starship bases, etc. Getting around the game has never been easier than it is now. Each system has its own economy and predominate race, and there's ample opportunity to exploit the universe's resources and the economy of its inhabitants so that you can profit and become a space god.

If you're looking for PvP then this is not the game for you. Go play EVE Online if that's your goal. Each game has their strengths and that is not a strength if this game. As a matter of fact it hardly exists at all. This game focuses on exploring planets themselves and EVE focuses on the bigger picture, and offers no on-foot experience of planets at all, and has a much larger focus on multiplayer, and is completely player-driven in every single aspect. This is kind of a hybrid of a single-player game offering multiplayer when it suits you.

They are polar opposites in what they focus on even though they are equally as vast. Both succeed at selling that "the universe is infinite!" feeling and both are incredible games. The difference here is there's no subscription :) 

This is one flat fee, free updates, and a dev team that has really proved that they care. What more can you ask for? :D

Either get it on G - 2 - A or on sale - it's worth $60 but I don't know why you'd buy it for $60 when you can get it for $30. Even on Steam this goes on sale for 50% off at least 5 times per year.

In a world saturated with crafting and base building sandbox's, No Man's Sky pretty much ticks everything that I could ask for in a game of this genre. I only have 81 hours invested in the game on PC, but closer to 1400 hours invested on my XBONE save. That should also tell you that I didn't experience the horrible launch that plagued this game when it was initially released, but for every minute and hour I've invested in this game has been absolutely worth it.

Sure, the combat is basic... to say the least. The sentinels don't really put up much of a fight. But that doesn't mean the inexperienced should be weary. They are bullet sponges. So make sure to have plenty of ammo. And until the recent updates, the ships have been all lack luster and a bit copy/paste. But they are all dynamic and leveled and can meant a lot when it comes to mining, trading, or ship to ship combat. 

BUT! The developer cares. Say what you will but they 1. Acknowledged they messed up 2. Apologized formally and 3. Have made all lifetime updates free, didn't abandon the game and continue to release new content, on average, I would say bi-quarterly, even during the COVID-19/2020 pandemic. 

Buy it. Don't wait for it to go on sale. Buy the dame game, I promise it's worth it. The amount of content, community support and developer support is worth the full price. If Minecraft, Empyrion - Galactic Survival, Rust, ARK: SE, Elite: Dangerous, or Grounded are games that you regularly enjoy, you will love No Man's Sky.

Overall, NMS is a good game if you enjoy exploration games.

The tone of the game is very trippy. Dialogue was definitely written while on drugs. The plot is strange, and I wasn't really a fan of it.  Colors are bright and flora and fauna is often bizarre. This game makes good screenshots and can be very pretty at times, if very unrealistic.  The world doesn't act like you would expect and some game mechanics that you just need to get used to. On normal difficulty though it's very forgiving and it's honestly pretty hard to screw up and get yourself stuck.

Exploration is fun. Eventually you run out of new planet types to explore and it gets repetitive, but this is easily 100+ hours into the game.

Ships are all pretty similar and upgrades are modular and don't really give you any customization. It's more a issue of how much space you dedicate to an upgrade type (shields, engine, weapons, etc) and the more space you use, the better it gets. I'm glad they added the option to increase cargo size because before that, getting a good ship required reloading until one with good stats randomly appeared and that was boring and a horrible game mechanic. Now you can actually upgrade a ship you like the look of instead.  I really wish there were cosmetic customization since you're pretty much stuck with how a ship looks when you get it.

Inventory management is still poor, although since they increased the storage capacity of storage units, it's much better.

Base building is actually quite good now and you can make all sorts of things, including underwater bases, although it takes a fair bit of time to get all the upgrades to actually build a full base.

There's a lot of stuff to do so if you're looking to burn a couple hundred hours on a game, it's a good option.

Inventory/management is pretty bad, you do slowly extend your slots as the game goes on but its way too limited at the start for how many different resources there are, with no simple way to store them you find yourself constantly having to delete resources to free up slots.  I don't think you should have unlimited inventory space but I also don't think it's good gameplay design forcing the player to destroy stuff they are going to have to go and farm again in 10 mins to make room just to be able to craft something, because there's nowhere else to store it if all slots are full and dropping = destroying.

A lot of planets are pretty samey early on - Have cold, radiation, heat levels which will slowly kill you and occasional storms that increase the severity but otherwise they have scattered ore, ruins and NPC outposts.  Every planet seems to have sodium, oxygen, ferrite and dihydrogen in abundance, the latter two are to make it impossible to get stranded on a planet as they can be used to make fuel and the former two are needed for life support systems.  I haven't seen if they get more diverse later on but have encountered a couple of exotic planets that are totally different to the usual setup, but so far the ones I have found are fairly meh as running around for 5 minutes on them it seems like you have seen everything there is to see.

Aside from the niggles it's still a solid game now, plenty to do and is very chill.  You don't really feel rushed to get on with the main story if you don't want to and can instead set up bases on different planets and explore/make money/get your reputation and upgrades up.  

Still definitely suffers from the grey goo problem of procedural generation - For gameplay purposes a lot of the generated content is exactly the same but slightly reskinned, but there is definitely enough unique content to keep the average person going for a while.

This game comes with a plephora of baggage regarding the fall and rise of the game, but I want to put all of that aside and review the game as simply a game, with no context around it.

No Man's Sky is a good game. It's pretty, cool, and creative. It's a galaxy-sized sandbox in which you can basically do whatever you want - explore the galaxy, discover new plants and creatures, fight space-pirates, connect with alien civillizations, build bases, make your fleet bigger, and more!
The visuals are nice, and the variety of different planets to explore and things to find is great.

This game is definitely not without flaws, though. Some issues I'd experienced in my playthrough are:
-Boring grinding: As you play, you'll meet different creatures and find new planets, but for the most part they're aesthetic changes and nothing else. You still spend the game walking around and holding the mouse trigger on stuff. There's heaps to unlock and discover, but I personally find the moment-to-moment gameplay of No Man's Sky a bit boring.
-Lack of challenge: The game makes you "feel" threatened, especially in the beginning of the game, but in reality this game is very not challenging. At time of writing, I've played this game for 44 hours and haven't died a single time, whether from running out of oxygen/thermal protection, or from land/space combat. I actually don't even know if dying is possible in No Man's Sky.
This kind of takes a lot away from the game, because if you're not threatened, why would you keep grinding away to get better stuff?
-Innacuracy: A personal gripe as a fan of astrophysics, but a lot of the things in the game don't make much sense. It's weird to find so many planets brimming with life, and it's odd to find so few oceans in those planets. Likewise, it's a bit sad there are no different gravitational fields on the different planets/moons.

While I personally didn't get to experience it, I bet the game really shines in multiplayer, as it seems like the perfect sandbox to play with pals and do some crazy stuff.
I'd still recommend this game for single player gamers, but maybe at a lower price point. The beginning is stellar, but it gets old after a bit.
Don't buy this game if you're looking for a challenging experience, or an accurate depiction of space and space travel.

TL;DR: If you like waiting while pointing a laser at things and constantly navigating menus, this game is for you. If you don't like those things (or are neutral about them) but want to explore the galaxy and find cool plants and animals, this game is not for you.

No Man's Sky bills itself as a game of exploration, survival, combat, and trading. It is actually a game of waiting and navigating menus. I have yet to see any combat or trading and very little exploration or survival, because at the beginning of the game you are tasked with a number of small missions that you need to do. These missions require you to point a laser at a series of objects and wait (and wait) while the laser breaks them down into materials, then navigate menus to start crafting, then navigate more menus because crafting things once isn't enough, then find more things to point your laser at (and wait...) to collect more materials. Eventually you will have to find things to point your laser at in order to recharge your laser (which also requires menu navigation).

Finding things to point your laser at involves a little exploration, but the planet you're on is so homogeneous that once you've found a dozen things to laser you probably won't care about exploring any more. Oh, and navigating the planet takes a long time, so once you've seen the few plants and animals that exist you're going to be seeing a lot more of those as you wait to find the right things to laser.

While you're waiting for your laser to finish breaking things down, it's possible that the radiation on the surface of the planet has whipped up into a storm, so now you must retrace your steps back to your ship. This is survival! It isn't really interesting, though, because planetary navigation isn't a challenge or puzzle. Just point yourself toward your ship and wait until you get there.

After an hour of the introductory menu navigation / crafting missions I was told to find an answer in the stars. I got in the ship, excited to finally be doing something potentially cool, but then once I exited the atmosphere I was instructed to go back down to the planet I had just come from-- there was a mysterious signal. It turned out to be an excuse for more lasering and menu navigation.  

One hour later (after dealing with a frustrating structure crafting menu navigation experience) I tried to leave the planet again (I had to go laser more things and navigate more menus to get more fuel for the ship). I was a little shocked that this worked, and finally excited that I'd get to see a new place! I followed the instructions to make the ship go faster... and then waited. Pretty streaks of color went past the cockpit. I waited a bit longer. Then I slowed down the ship and rotated around to see planets! Including the planet that I had just left, which was by far the closest one. I pointed myself at the next closest planet, got up to top speed, and the game told me it would take one minute and forty-three seconds to get there. 1:43... during which I could look at the streaks of color, or even navigate the crafting menus. What joy.

Once on the new planet I got out of the ship and started moving about, only to find that the fauna and flora and minerals there were more or less the same as the place I'd just left, just with a different color palette. It was at this point that I closed the game, probably for good.

Those of you who like this game, please tell me: What am I supposed to be doing during the many long, dull minutes I have spent pointing my laser at objects? Why do I have to navigate menus to build piece A and piece B in order to navigate more menus to construct equipment C? If I have all the raw materials, why can't I just build equipment C? What is fun about menu navigation?

Bonus criticism: The menu navigation in VR is quite annoying. Many of the menus are attached to your hands, so you're trying to hold one hand absolutely still while you point at the right selection with your other hand. It's not difficult, exactly, but it is a needless "challenge" that adds to the amount of time you spend navigating menus.

I had no interest in this game when it first came out after the bad launch, but I bought it on sale after I watched an Internet Historian video about how the devs put their noses to the grindstone and kept working on the game to fulfill their original promises instead of taking the money and running because I thought that mentality should be encouraged.
That being said, after putting in about 200 hours between VR and flat modes, it's definitely worth what I paid and I'd buy it again at full price.

If you're looking for AAA cinematic cut scenes with a deep solo story you're not going to find that here, although they have added a good bit of lore and a few narrative quest lines that are mostly text based. This is ultimately an exploration game so don't go in expecting it to be something it's not. Think something like GTA in space but with a 90/10 side quest/main quest ratio. 

As far as procedural generation goes, repeats of certain flora and fauna are quite common but you can't expect them to handcraft an entire universe, I imagine that's also why the game install is less than 10GB which is nice. 

Playing solo is fun and quite immersive in VR and there's enough variety to keep you busy for quite some time, however if you're playing with others and trying to keep up I think flat mode is the way to go because you can perform the more grindy tasks much more quickly than in VR. 

On that note, I think the addition of multiplayer is where the game really shines if you have a few friends who play the game. It's pretty easy to just hop into each other's games and interact with voice chat without having to use any external programs.

There's a community hub called Space Anomaly that you can summon in-game that functions much like the Tower in Destiny where you can pick up missions and form 4 player fireteams or try to complete them solo.

I often hear from people who haven't played the game that the graphics are too "cartoony" which I can only assume is based on the box art. IMO the game itself looks no more "cartoony" than Mass Effect, Halo or Destiny and with the graphics settings cranked up looks pretty great on my laptop with a GeForce 1060 6GB.

So bottom line, will you get tired of this game playing solo and start seeing a good bit of repetition between 30-40 hours of gameplay? Probably.
But with online multiplayer and a couple friends it becomes a pretty engaging online sandbox that can be extended indefinitely, whether that be by picking up and completing nexus quests or cooperative Minecraft-like base building or trying to kill each other.

Bought this game since some friends had also picked it up and thought it would be fun for a while, I knew of it's bad reputation but also heard about all the updates and work the devs had put in to redeem it, plus the steam reviews are now at very positive. After putting a good chunk of time into it, overall I think its a clunky and tedious experience. I did have some fun with it, but it definitely feels like a game that was stitched together over the course of 5 years. 

There is plenty of "content" but it's all quite samey and the gameplay pretty much boils down to being a grind, and not the fun kind like say factorio or other sandbox/survival games. I feel like since the game was so anemic on launch they added a bunch of stuff that just takes forever to do in order to pad out the play time. For example, every single part of your base has to be researched, every wall tile, ceiling tile, door, room shape, hallway, window and everything else, of which there are dozens and dozens of. This means that you can't just put in the time to build an awesome looking base, instead you have to first spend hours aimlessly roaming from one buried data pod to the next in order to get enough data to buy the parts that you need. It completely kills the enthusiasm for what could be a great feature because it's gated by a huge grind of monotonous nonsense. This also applies to researching new vehicles, upgrades, industrial machines and whatever else except those are even more expensive.

The gameplay mostly consists of searching around the galaxy for new materials and components to upgrade your gear, ship, and vehicles. As you unlock better stuff, you need rarer materials to do so. This sounds interesting, and for a bit it is because you expand out into space stations, new planets, and new systems on the search. However eventually it devolves into an annoying game of inventory management, lists of things you need for this or that, and the constant feeling that you forgot to pick something up or buy something when you were there last. There's just a ton of shit to keep track of, with upgrades and tech modules for your suit, your ship, your base, the three classes of vehicles, your multitool, your freighter, and so on each requiring their own components to craft. And you have so little inventory to work with at least to start. It feels less like gameplay and more like constantly running back and forth from the grocery store as you forgot some ingredient for dinner and now you have to try and remember where you saw it last. You can quickly teleport to all the space stations you've been to but they all sell different things, or you have to look for planetary outposts that sell the rarer ones, or you have to stop on some planet for 5 minutes to scrape up one of the 3 unique resources each spawns with, it's all very brain dead.

What's more frustrating is that a ton of the upgrades are pretty much just convenience factor. Bigger inventory space, longer life support, longer sprinting, more effecient engines so you don't have to spend as much time mining fuel. I spent most of my play time effectively upgrading stuff that was just to smooth out an annoyance. Why even have a sprint meter in a game about exploring? because then they can put in an upgrade for it and count it as more content. Some of these things I feel are just hampering my exploration experience in the name of adding some kind of progression by getting stuff to unhamper it. Then by the time I got to the point where I had the upgrades to make exploring fun, I realized there was no reason to explore anymore.

The thing is that I kept going, I was getting that addictive urge to keep grinding just for grindings sake. But then I realized I wasn't actually having much fun doing it, so I stopped playing. I don't see the game ever really escaping this kind of gameplay loop and it's not for me. Maybe if you're a runescape player.

When No Man's Sky was first released, I thought that Sean Murray with his lies and his team would take all the money and disappear. Hello Games didn't run away and instead, they updated the game over the years. Since 2016 they introduced bases, then vehicles, a new story-line, multiplayer, VR, and much more.

But with updates come bugs. Most of the bugs tend to be ironed out in the next few patches so that's fine I guess.

EXPLORATION

Exploration in the game is fun at first but when you explored all types of planets (toxic, scorched, cold, etc.) all the other planets feel almost the same. Since the fauna and the flora aren't procedurally generated, you can see some of the fauna or flora on other planets. The space stations look almost the same in every galaxy and every star system. The environment on the planets is boring because you don't have anything to explore. There are no rivers, waterfalls, volcanoes, etc. There is nothing special about the environment. 

SOLAR SYSTEMS

Solar systems lack quite a few things. E.g there are no gas giants in the game. There are way fewer moons than planets. There is no climate on the planets. And I'm pretty sure that there are more examples that I forgot.

VR

I have tried VR and it's not bad, but the controls and the UI are a little bit weird because it was not made from the ground up, but imported from the pc version with VR controls and some changes. They should focus a little bit more on VR. e.g: move the information about the planet, health, etc. on the player's hand (something like in half-life: Alyx).

CONCLUSION

I like No Man's Sky. It has a lot of potential, but I think that the developers should focus more on improving the gameplay mechanics and improving the planets/solar systems instead of adding something brand new into the game. This game has a lot of annoying little inconveniences that could be fixed pretty easily. But it's still quite playable and enjoyable, so I have mixed feelings about this game.

I probably would not have enjoyed this game when it first came out because it was so empty, judging by the experiences of others here, but starting after so many updates and bug fixes means that I had a much cleaner and more robust introduction to the game than the early reviewers and I am really enjoying it 120 someodd hours in.

In fact one of the only criticisms that I have is that all the new additions seem to have been added fully expecting the player to have already experienced the game along the way, so there is no hierarchy of mechanics when it comes to acquisition and introduction. Whatever "golden path" of introduction they may have had at launch has become a maze of paths the crisscross into a web. The various tutorial missions overlap each other, sometimes interfering with each other, and the mission system is hard-pressed to keep up with what you've already done or what you need to do with so many paths in play at once - add to that the layer of multiplayer in the form of a centralized hub for all players to visit (after a certain amount of progress through a tutorial of course) that lets players break the chains of the tutorials and acquire pretty much anything they want whenever they want, and it's a fairly chaotic mess trying to figure out what to do next, or how to do it.

But then that's half the fun of an open universe - figuring out what to do when you can do so much it at least *feels* like you can do anything. And hey this is the internet age so that's what forums and wikis are for. :)

To answer the questions I had when I started:

Is the game a grind? Well sort of - I mean it's a grindy game for sure but it's not that there's a lot of grind between game parts it's that the grind *is* the game. It's a game about making what you want out of what you can find so you can do what you want in a vast universe you can explore and make your mark on in real time. Which means that when you want to make something you need to have what is needed, both in terms of the knowledge of how to make it and the materials to do so - if you don't have it you have to get it. Thus half the game is managing your inventory and acquiring what you need for the next steps in whatever master plan you're working toward. And to me, at least, that's a lot of fun.

Are there bugs? Yes, quite a few actually (I'm writing this while I wait for Steam to sync up because it just hard crashed on me) but they are uncommon, the developer fixes them regularly, autosave happens every time you leave a ship, and sometimes the bugs can be beneficial. So they're not bad enough to be really irritating. 

Is the universe empty? Sometimes yes, sometimes no - a lot of the mechanics and updates they've been implementing have been aiming toward populating the universe, including the new(ish) multiplayer system that is 100% voluntary and seems to be largely cooperative (haven't delved in too deep there because I don't trust random players and I'm waiting for a friend to spin up on the game to join me).

What about lore and story? Is there any? Yes there's quite a bit scattered around and it keeps hinting at more. At the early stage I'm at it's all very mysterious and seems quite far-reaching, but it's rather confusing and bits often lack any kind of resolution or way to follow up - but then I haven't delved far down the apparent primary mission storyline because I'm having too much fun running around discovering things and getting rich. Perhaps that's where the meat of the storyline lies - either way it's there to be pursued if you want or ignored if you don't and it's distinctly eerie sometimes. I'm an RPG story nut so I'm hoping it's there once I'm ready, but then again it's not necessarily vital if I'm this addicted without it.

Is the action good? It depends - ground combat is ok and at least feature rich to compensate for the meh (it's also buggy when it gets too difficult which makes it more survivable), the 'horror mode' style of derelict freighter exploration they just introduced in the last update is actually very engaging it's just pricey to get into (you have to buy locations for lots of units so don't expect to do it until you're already pretty rich), but the space combat is kind of a joke. I was all jazzed about being able to play a Freelancer style open world dogfighter using my HOTAS flightstick again, but this was not that. The space component has no affordance for vector thrust so it just feels like a plane you can fly backwards, the bounding boxes are bizarre, and it has no support for anything other than keyboard/mouse, so hardcore space shooter it ain't. If you want that then Elite: Dangerous might be more your bag (my buddy spinning up on this game calls it "Landing: The Game") but if the mechanics of space combat aren't critical to you then it's fun and pretty easy overall and a very rich place to explore. And if you actively dislike space combat then never fear - once you get used to how it works and how the AI fights (basically it's dumb as rocks) it at least won't be an impediment to your enjoyment of the universe.

This is currently my favorite game. 
When I heard all of the amazing and incredible things that were going to be in this game when it was released, I was sold! And I pre-ordered it. Yep, full $60 pre-order back 2016. I couldn't wait to play it! And then when it did come out I tried to play it on my "gaming" laptop, but found my CPU graphics weren't good enough to play it. As time went on, I saw so many people up in arms about how terrible it was, and I felt cheated and sad even though I still had never played it. Even after I had a halfway decent, proper gaming PC I still didn't play it because I had been CONVINCED by the internet that it was a bad game made by bad people who didn't care about their potential consumers.

Flash forward to a few months ago right around when the quarantines started; I fell in love with the game after a friend of mine tried numerous times to get me to play it. I finally gave in and tried it. And it's great.

At the time of this review I have over 120 hours in No Man's Sky. A lot of it spent grinding for an S-Class freighter only to settle on the largest A-Class I could find. Twice.. But I have started my own, proper, base. And there is a unique beauty and tranquility to the universe that Hello Games has created inside this game.

For the player that likes a super amazing story that is just so in depth that the characters LITERALLY grab you through your monitor and drag you into the game? This probably isn't for you. BUT, I found that it does have a unique story unlike others that I have played that does immerse you in it's universe. It's a story that I found makes me appreciate reality and the beauty outside more than I might have before.

The sandbox experience is very cool too. I haven't gotten super in depth with it, but I'm getting there. I've seen some SUPER creative builds in No Man's Sky on YouTube. Apparently you can do a lot with it.

My favorite thing about the game, though, is how stupid big it is. Seriously. I'm used to games where you look at the map of where you can go, and sure there's a good bit of stuff to do, but after a while you get bored or run out of places to go. In No Man's Sky if you get bored you pull up your Galactic Map, pic a star, go there and there are a brand new set of planets to explore. Or you can set out to learn the entire language of one of the three main species in the game. Or there are quests in the Nexus that you can do with other people. Or... whatever you want, I guess.

To me, this game is different. It's unlike any other game I've played, and I encourage anyone who is considering whether or not they should buy this game, buy it. Probably on sale, but I don't think you'd be wasting your money if you bought this at full price either.

Hello Games is working HARD to atone for their mistakes in 2016. And it shows. After spending literally hundreds of dollars on DLC for Destiny ALONE, I really appreciate a game developer/company that updates the game with new content for FREE. FOUR YEARS AFTER THE GAME CAME OUT. Seriously, Hello Games could have take the literal millions that they made off of the pre-orders alone and just disappeared off the face of the earth. But they didn't. They've worked hard to make No Man's Sky the game they originally said they would, the game they promised to thousands of people. And I think they have.

TL:DR... Good game, buy it.

The save system on this game makes almost *zero* sense.  I have played both on Xbox and on PC, collectively for about 25 hours total.  Already,  I have suffered the following two significant loses:

1) On Xbox, I received an error pop-up regarding saving to the cloud, once.  After the error the game continued to run and continued to say 'Restore point saved' anytime I left my ship.  So, I assumed the error was a fluke and continued to play for another 5 hours that night.  When I went to resume my game the next day I realized that *NONE* of those 5 hours actually saved.  Poof, gone.  Why were no more errors reported after the first and why didn't the game actually save anything and then sync the progress up to the cloud the next chance it had?

2) On PC, I experienced a random crash to desktop after spending 2+ hours collecting resources to buy a new multi-tool.  As soon as it happened I felt that sinking feeling because I absolutely knew all of the progress was lost.  Re-launch the game and sure enough, 2 hours gone because of a second reason entirely out of my control.

So, after experiencing the above two game failure I have lost roughly 6 out of 25 hours (~25%) of progress.  What a frustratingly terrible introduction to a game that I have otherwise been enjoying.  It does make me wonder why the save system is so moronically designed.  It makes me wonder, specifically, why:

1) There is no true manual save that allows the player to save immediately and exit.  Sometimes we have to respond to situations outside of the game, you know,  in the real world.  Apparently, the game designers think everyone can spare the time to run back to their ship, just to save. Strange.

2) There is no auto-save, every 5 minutes or so, to address cases where the game and/or the PC crash.  In a perfect world, no game, app or PC would ever crash.  We don't live in that world yet, hence why auto-save has been a thing for well over 2 decades now.  Auto-save in No Man's Sky? Nope.  Why? Who knows...

The game is fun despite such an enormous oversight.  If you don't mind a game that also provides an unpredictable amount of RNG in regards to whether or not your progress will be saved then go ahead and buy it, I guess.

I bought this game at a huge discount fully expecting to return it within an hour.

2 weeks later I'm alternating playing the game in VR and PC for hours each day just to experience every nook and cranny. I played a little of this game when it came out 4 years ago and I can confidently say this is a completely different game from the ground up, huge improvement over the nightmare it was on launch.

Pros : Never running out of interesting little quests, puzzles, general to-do items. If you get bored doing one thing it feels like there's 1000 others to take up your time. The game can become as slow or as faced paced as you want, from hunting down bounties on space pirates to happily cultivating a little farm with some alien friends on your base, or chatting up other races on space stations.

Cons: BUGGY AS HELL in VR. Honestly not a bad thing sometimes, as VR mode allows you to teleport HUGE distances and save on life support resources, as well as makes combat and flying your ship a thousand percent easier. The things that suck in VR (base building, finding specific resources on scanner, crafting) can be easily remedied by switching to PC version, so I compartment my time accordingly. Also do NOT play this game in VR if you get motion sickness, I imagine it'd be pretty barfy.

If you've heard about / played this game on launch - the procedurally generated planets are still same-y and boring, so if you're looking forward to a huge diversity of flora and fauna, this still ain't it. However I feel like this is a relatively more moot point now that the game has more content than at launch.

TL;DR : if you're on the fence, get this game on sale and give it a try for <2 hours, you might be pleasantly surprised at how much has changed

This game is great as a concept, but the execution is still lacking after four years from initial launch.

The biggest problem is that for a "game about exploration and survival in an infinite procedurally generated universe", there is surprisingly little variety of places to explore and very few things that actually threaten your survival.

First, the exploration: the universe is very cookie-cutter and immutable. There are 7 main planet types (jungle, frozen, fire, desert, radioactive, toxic, empty) and about a dozen rare "glitch planet" types. All of these are very homogeneous, single-biome planets with no large-scale features such as mountain ranges, deserts, polar ice caps, rivers or cities, and every two planets of the same type are very similar to each other. Oceans and caves are the same everywhere in the universe and don't depend on the planet's type. Each inhabited planet has the same set of buildings; each type of building very closely follows its template. There is no random unique loot to find like in Borderlands - all of the loot in buildings consists of basic supplies that you can buy at any space station and small amounts of currencies. You can encounter random crashed spaceships to repair, but the only ways the spaceships differ is inventory space and appearance. Every space station interior is the same, with the only variable being which of the three alien races you find inside and which resources are for sale. Although each star system is theoretically unique, there's no compelling reason to explore beyond your immediate neighborhood, because you will likely encounter all planet types (with the possible exception of glitch planets) in the first dozen or so systems you visit, and the resources available on a planet are fully determined by its type and the star system. There is a decent variety of creatures, but there is no way to consistently find them on a planet. The universe is not meaningfully affected by player actions - you can dig a hole or build a large base and it will stay there, but you can't meaningfully influence a star system's economy or participate in any sort of space conflict other than an inconsequential pirate skirmish. The claim from the store description that "the galaxy is a living, breathing place" is simply not true - it is completely static and exploring it is more like playing a racing game with 20 tracks on an infinite random repeat than wandering around in Minecraft.

Next, the survival. I think including this in the short description was downright misleading. This aspect is only relevant in the first few hours of the game. Once you get a reasonable amount of cash, you can buy all the essential resources from a space station and it's just a waste of time to mine resources from planets - just grow plants in your freighter, craft high value products from them, and buy the things you need from traders. If you buy all five environmental protection upgrades, it is trivial to survive indefinitely on any planet, even on 'extreme worlds' (ones with particularly hazardous environments). The only plausible ways you can die despite your best efforts is by deliberately attacking Sentinels (robots that guard certain locations) or deliberately triggering Biological Horror (aliens that spawn when you destroy a specific item) and then trying to fight it off instead of running back to your ship. In practice, the most common way I died is from an explosion of my own plasma grenade when fighting off Biological Horror.

Land combat is pretty awkward. Weapons are crafted as upgrades for universal multi-tools rather than found as loot, which seems like a mistake. You are supposed to defend yourself from the largest Sentinel robots with a personal force field, but the robots are so tall that they can shoot you from above, and the force field only protects you in the front - you can't tilt it upwards. You can't clear robots from a planet - they will keep spawning indefinitely like the police in GTA. Space combat is there, but it's not engaging at all. Point at enemy ship, shoot it until it explodes, repeat. Pirates are not a real danger even when flying a cargo ship with no upgrades. It's not possible to destroy any capital ships and there are no fleet versus fleet battles.

Progression is largely based on grind, some of which is moreover artificially slowed down by frustratingly slow dialog menus and animations (for example, you need to wait for your spaceship to turn around after landing on a freighter or a space station before you can exit it). The one non-grindy way to get ahead is to find a crashed starship with significantly larger inventory than your own and repair it.

On a technical level, the game is rather buggy. Some objects sometimes fail to spawn, explosion effects randomly just stop working until you restart the game, plant draw distance is essentially random even with everything set to Ultra, texture pop-in is a constant problem even with a high end graphics card. These problems are especially pronounced when driving the Roamer and Pilgrim exocraft (vehicles), which are too fast for the game to catch up with loading plants and rocks. I also encountered a few crashes.

There is a story and some in-universe lore to discover, but they are rather thin. The primary purpose of the main quest is to collect portal glyphs that let you warp to arbitrary planets.

This game is no doubt far better than when it initially launched, but due to the limited variety, it still doesn't fulfill its grand promise. There are specific elements that are done really well, such as creatures and the derelict freighters from the most recent update, but the whole is less than the sum of its parts.

I did not play this game at launch, so I'm going to review it based on the game it is today. This review is going to be relatively spoiler-free.

[b]Current Update as of this review:[/b] Desolation
[b]My Bias:[/b] I enjoy exploration games that let me do whatever I want like Subnautica
[b][u]Current PC Specs as of this review (For your comparison):[/u][/b]
[b]CPU[/b] - Intel Core i5-6600K 3.5 GHz Quad-Core Processor
[b]GPU[/b] - Sapphire Radeon R9 390 8GB Nitro Video Card
[b]RAM[/b] - Corsair Vengeance LPX 16GB of DDR4-2800 CL15 Memory
[b]SSD[/b] (Where I put the game) - Crucial MX500 1TB

[b]The Pros:[/b]
+ Consistent Updates - Instead of dropping the game like a bag of bricks, Hello Games has decided to keep rolling with it and provide new and interesting updates to the ever-growing playerbase. The game already feels solid, so every update is just a bonus at this point. The developer actually takes direct bug requests via their zendesk website to continually fix/improve the game.
+ Radiant Missions - I can choose to take missions or I can choose to skip them. The radiant missions offered add to the gameplay and make it easier to create goals for myself in-game.
+Base-Building - You can create a base however you like from a gigantic tower to a tiny hovel. The developer could probably add even more options, but there is a lot there already to create the base of your dreams.
+Exploration - There are literally trillions of planets in this game. Each solar system seems to have at least one interesting planet with something I have not seen before.

[b]The Could Be Improved:[/b]
+/- Multiplayer - Somehow adding a network connection with a friend or randoms causes the game to lag heavily sometimes. In the case of my friend, it would sometimes break whole aspects of their game - not allowing them to progress unless they completely left our gaming session and tried again on their own.
+/- Main Missions - They feel like they could be fleshed out just a bit more. There is a lot of interesting aspects about the gameplay and story that I would like to see improved on/added to. My favorite characters should not just stop talking to me because I finished their quest line.
+/- Enemies - The AI for this game is not very advanced, but I did not expect a whole lot with a procedurally-generated game. I would like to see more aggression and more health to make the AI a bit more challenging to deal with.
+/- Variety - The subreddit loves to constantly harp on this, but I actually agree with them. After a while, a lot of planets feel very similar with biodiversity and environment. It would be nice to see some more of the interesting planets as described in the storylines like blood oceans or giant gelatnous mega-fauna that absorb everything in their path. I got tired of seeing the same venus flytraps/bursting plants and your run of the mill predators. However, anomalous planets are incredibly interesting, and something that I always went out of my way to go see.

[b]The Bad:[/b]
-Enemy Attacks - Certain enemies are able to attack through objects. This is incredibly annoying, but thankfully avoidable once you figure out which enemies do what.
-Exploits/Bugs/Glitches - This game is definitely not Bethesda-level of keeping the game a buggy mess, but it definitely needs improvement. Please remember to report the bugs to Hello Games directly on their zendesk website and they may actually fix issues (see Consistent Updates under [b]The Pros[/b]). Making money (units) is trivial once you figure out how to cheese the economy, but thankfully the game still ramps up costs over your playtime to make it worthwhile to do different things.

Overall, I loved the game and will definitely come back for future updates.

There are so many different ways one can play this game, and I'm sure most of the reviews here touch on them, but I'm gonna go a step further, for you, my review-reading friend.  I am going to address exactly which of the many featured playstyles of this game may be attracting you, and let you know how worth it that aspect of the game is if you're considering purchasing right now.

Story-driven Gameplay:  If you're wondering about this, there are better games.  I recommend The Outer Worlds.  NMS has some really cool story stuff in it, almost existentially amazing at times, but the act of progressing said stories is difficult to enjoy when you're preoccupied with the dozens of other opportunites knocking on your HUD, and conversely kind of boring when you focus solely on said storyline.

Exploration:  The irony of the basic infinite nature of gameplay design in NMS is that you play more than long enough to start feeling like you've already seen everything.  I'd say that's cool, because it takes a LONG time to start feeling that way and you've had a lot of fun for those hours, BUT you've also only just explored a microfraction of what should be vastly different regions of multiple galaxies.  The scale of difference is not large enough to accomodate the scale of the NMS universe.  This has always been my biggest complaint about this game, and it is obviously not even on development rader.  Maybe it's being saved for NMS2 technology?

TRADING:  Trading in this game is actually pretty brilliant, and easy.  All you need is cargo space and a quick google search will give you the definitive chart for plotting trade routes based on system type and quality.  You'll want to get the economy scanner upgrade as soon as possible, then use it from your X menu to find the nearest Trading Post in a system, at which the profit/loss margins are better than on stations.

SPACE COMBAT:  Until your heart is content.  The plethora of upgrades and configurations that you can build into a single ship, not to mention that you can amass your own fleet of optional ships to pilot, as well as your freighter and all of the frigates you can hire to do space stuff to bring you space stuff.  As far as continuity, that's another story.  You pick a fight or a fight picks you, you pew pew, and then basically repeat with not much of a consequence other than possible racial reputation changes that can be fixed by doing a few "scan 5 minerals" missions, so meh.

BUILDING:  This part of the game has gotten WAY too much attention in my opinion, so forgive my lack of enthusiasm for this facet of gameplay in a game that touted itself as such a huge galaxy, so much to explore, blah blah blah now pick 1 planet, but your one base on it, and here lets make a new kind of station that warps in right where you want it and makes it so you basically never have to leave your wittle system.  Yeah, you can build stuff.  Prefabricated building parts you put together, run wires for electric, hire dudes to give you a few more "offical" back and forth item grabbing quests, because there aren't enough of those ... to get you some base building type upgrade stuff.  It's actually very well fleshed out in terms of meaningful construction as dictated by the little story it FORCES you to go through in order to be able to build everything ... but practically, it's really pretty useless.  Yeah yeah, activated indium farm, congrats on that epic method of making the game boring for yourself.

I think that about does it.  This is my favorite game ever.  Hope ya like it.

Reviews.128001:
There are moments in NMS where you are struck by the beauty and excitement of exploration, whether it's finally discovering an Eden-like planet, encountering a mind-bending ever-shifting being of pure geometry, or simple seeing the shimmering maw of a black hole up close for the first time. These moments, sadly, are few and far between, absolutely lost in the swamp of utter tedium that is the rest of the game. 

I've played a lot of glorified inventory managers and stat trackers in my time, some "boring" or repetitive games can be excellent relaxing time-sinks. NMS would absolutely be one of them, and in fact still could be if you have the patience of a saint and don't mind an eternity of convoluted search/collect/fix tasks routinely punctuated and set back by bug after bug after bug. In the end, once the novelty's worn off, it's just...annoying. There isn't any kind of real reward or incentive to keep going after getting stuck in a conversation screen/galaxy map/menu *again* and having to reload *again* to do your one thousand mini-tasks *again*. I have ~65 hours logged; at least 10 of those were reloads and attempts at workarounds (and another 10 when I fell asleep with it running). I couldn't use the Portals in the game without catastrophic effects almost every time, costing me time and rewards from the main game and Nexus missions. 

The final straw was loading it up today, finding myself in a completely random system that wasn't my last save or anywhere near it (600LY from the centre, which I've never even been close to), opening up the galaxy map...and getting stuck in it, not even able to hit ESC. And not for the first time. 

Even when it's not buggy, it's still frustrating and unenjoyable to be forced to do repetitive menial tasks like repairing your frigates (one of the worst mechanics in the game, btw), only to be mobbed by pirates because you've dared to exist near a freighter for more than 5 seconds, or needing to scan x amount of animals but every planet within 1000 lightyears has no fauna and roughly one million angry Sentinels. The quests you are given are completely trivial, and the difficulty completely artificial. I don't feel challenged or even particularly engaged, ever, just constantly inconvenienced.

The gameplay is okay. I actually like the scanning and scavaging part of it, it can be very relaxing if you're able to find a place to do it uninterrupted. I love my jetpack, especially with big upgrades. Building is easy and fairly fun, you can make some very useful devices and nice bases. Flying is, for the most part, hell. It's not worth owning more than one conventional space craft at a time, unless you want to have a collection. The frigate/freighter mechanic is cool, and a great way to make boatloads of units very quickly...if you can stand the constant repairs and the total gracelessness of the recruitment process.

The dialogue and writing is usually pretty good, I like a lot of the casual dialogue with NPC and the lore is genuinely interesting, but there's a cognitive dissonance between glorious, dramatic reveals and secrets and monologues vs the reality of slamming into the side of a mountain because the landing sequence works when you need/want it to about 5% of the time, key NPCs like the Armourer not spawning, or coming back to base to realise the terraforming you did to build it has somehow reversed and there's a hill growing through your science quarters. There's nothing to carry the story on, so it just seems sort of disjointed. 

I'm impressed with the crossplay and multiplayer elements, to an extent. Teaming up to do missions or sharing abandoned freighter finds is fun, and the community seem chill and generous (it's not unusual to go to the Nexus and have strangers randomly gift you nice things, or to have message pods with tips left near plot points), but actually exploring and hanging out felt clumsy and boring. 

Honestly, it feels like the Alpha release of a promising game. Considering it was released 4 years ago and has been in production ever since...I'm completely underwhelmed, regardless of how far it's come. I commend the team for continuing to work on this game with my whole heart, but it's also the first game I've ever requested a refund on (which I didn't get, obviously, but figured it was worth a try). It's too annoying and disruptive to be a very chill exploration game, but too boring and aimless to be any kind of sci-fi adventure game either.

However, I also bought this game for my partner and he seems to really be enjoying it, so it's very much as case of "your mileage my vary". He agrees it's buggy and tedious, but he has a higher bullshit tolerance than I do, and he's a bit of a completionist. Basically, if you are patient and NMS sounds like your kinda game, it probably is! It's fun to fart around in for a few hours, but don't expect smooth sailing. 

Worth getting at a heavy discount, but the £20 I paid was still definitely too much.

No man's sky is the greatest story of redemption in the video game industry
contrary to others i never refunded the game, mainly because i actually enjoyed the first 10'ish hours of gameplay when it first came out, so i just forgot about it and left it in the deepest corners of my library where it went to collect digital dust for two years.
then i heard more and more news of the game getting the support that Hello Games promised, getting a story, a base system, a almost complete overhaul to many things in the game and the more time went on the longer the game got supported.
i was initially very skeptical about the redeemability of This game, mainly because the backlash from the public at large was so insanely negative and i saw this game get roasted from all corners of the internet, with the dev studio accused of making a cash grab of a game like many others before.
but slowly, steadily, gently Hello Games chipped away at their bad reputation, and now are considered by the majority of gamers as "redeemed", this game is insanely fun now, it has a LOT of content in it and there is so much more that hello games wants to put in this.
i believe that the developers did not intend initially to release the game the way they did and they've remade the game in a way that fits what their initial vision for the game was.
Now for a scoring of no man's sky in july 2020, here is my opinion:

PROS
this game has a insanely complex procedural generation, the complexity that a world can reach after they've added so much content is insane
The story, while i think it takes itself a tad too seriously, is still enjoyable and it finally gives the players a proper objective to follow that isn't the classic and vague "get to the center of the galaxy duh", i like what they did here.
the online components and base building added a whole new facet to this game, it gives it replayability, something it was gravely missing when it first came out, its almost like building homes in different biomes in minecraft, only that the biomes are much more important to the gameplay, you could put yourself at a challenge by building your base on a inhospitable planet with a lot of resources or go for a peaceful planet that doesn't pose much of a threat.
the game's style is clean and recognizable, nothing too impressive graphics wise but the game truly does look stunning again and again, the care the devs put into making some things look beautiful is obvious: a giant freighter crashed into the ground in the middle of a valley with a thick fog, a abandoned space station with a dead space mood permeating it, beautiful snowy mountain ranges comparable with the alps, colorful planets with even more colorful moons, this game sure has some nice looking panoramas.
also the audio design is impeccable, every sound in the game feels carefully crafted to fit into the style of this game seamlessly.

CONS
the early game still feels tedious, its slow and painful at best, taking off your first planet is always very difficult
sometimes the generation still feels repetitive and barren, if you were to play no man's sky for the sake of exploration you'd probably feel the game becoming repetitive already after the first 10'ish systems explored
Combat still feels dumb, there are little enemy types and they become trivial after you unlock good weapons and are frustrating until then

WHAT THE DEVELOPERS SHOULD FOCUS ON TO MAKE THIS AS GOOD OF A GAME AS IT POSSIBLY CAN BE
Make taking off your first planet faster and less tedious
Enrich the flora and fauna generation even more, the original trailer had some insanely well made scenery with beautiful fauna and flora every where, make the fauna feel like its adapted to its environment more, like some slime mold that lives in extreme environments, or trees that walk, stationary creatures that filter the air and so on, there is a lot of potential that still has to be uncovered with creature and flora generation, also make it so that researching these lifeforms can unlock new and unique crafting recipes, maybe create a research system where you bring specimens that you've put in your ship from far away to be studied in more detail!
The caves need a overhaul, add more complexity to them and more incentives to explore them, also create some unique dungeons that appear underground and make enemies for the new dungeons.
the game still feels grindy in some parts, streamline how you obtain currency and new upgrades.
Add More and more early game augments that let you move fast on ground.
Add proper biomes for the planets, depending on latitude and how close they are to the star, also make stars something that actually exists in the systems, with planets that are too close to their star becoming tidally locked having one face always facing the star and another never facing it 

I wish the best of luck to the developers for all of their future endeavors and i believe that no man's sky is every year becoming a better and better game, good job.

This game is now praised for being good after the travesty of the launch. I will say this, it is now a good game, but it is still not really good like Subnautica. 

Pros:
*Amazing first few hours
*Crafting system is pretty good
*Base building
*Exploration has been revamped, and is now far better
*Farting around doing random things is the best part of this game
*Multiplayer and Co-op have now been added, with a public discovery system
*Devs are hellbent on adding new content.

Cons:
*The procedural generation system has its limits. Most of the planets look very similar, and don't have a lot of depth.
*Too easy to get stacked. And once you do, the game really isn't fun anymore. (I had over 300 million units in just 3 hours of gameplay.)
*Alien languages are dealt out in small pieces, requiring around 20 hours of going through systems to learn all words of a single race. (Note: My play time is on one save file, so after 31 hours I haven't even completed one language yet.)
*Gathering resources becomes obsolete when you can just buy anything you need, seeing as how it is far to easy to get filthy rich in the game.
*Getting all of the best equipment is too easy. Requiring no effort on your end except waiting in a wealthy system for a good ship, and when it comes to the second save the freighter mission, it can be exploited to get a guaranteed S class capital ship.
*Storyline is incredibly weak.

The best part about this game is its opening sequence and its base building. The fact that the developers are committed to making the game better is very good. I would not recommend this game in its current state simply due to the fact that there is not much to do once you become a god. Wait a few more years, or until they fix the progression system to purchase. 4/10
Reviews.128269:
In short, it’s a rocky start to an enjoyable experience.

Initially, very little is actually explained through in-game means. Once you start out you’ll want to build a base or a vehicle, only to find you can’t immediately and most blueprints are locked behind a confusing progression system with various ways to approach it that isn’t explained well. 

The quest system is confusing. Within an hour of starting you have three different main quests all pulling you in different directions, all leading to different unlocks and story paths.

The inventory management is a headache. Your suit, ships, vehicles, freighter and bases all have separate inventories that are managed independently without any way to check them remotely. Keeping track of what you have and where it is is a nightmare.

Despite its faults, once you get going and get a firm grasp on the mechanics and a few unlocks under your belt, the game is really enjoyable. 

Exploring hazardous planets in your environmentally-sealed exocraft or rocketing around uncharted worlds with your jetpack and rocket boots is a really enjoyable experience.

Learning alien vocabulary is a surprisingly enjoyable hobby. At first all aliens speak gibberish to you and your character just vaguely guesses at what they want. From exploring you start learning words and eventually you’ll be able to completely understand them. This comes in handy when you come across abandoned alien bases, where to get the most out of them you have to actively understand the alien’s language.

For VR headset owners, the VR mode works surprisingly well and feels as if the game was developed for VR.

In short, it’s an incredibly rough first twelve or so hours, but once you start understand the game’s mechanics more it’s actually a really fun experience.

When I was a kid I played a peculiar French game called L'Arche du Captain Blood. You assumed the role of a forlorn star-ship captain who is trying to track down his lost clones by travelling through space and conversing with strange alien beings. The art style was like if Mandelbrot and HR Geiger got-it-on in a haunted abattoir, and it had strange intro music by Jean-Michel Jarre that sounded like a Casio SK-1 having a seizure. No Man's Sky is kind of like if Captain Blood was remade, expanded upon, and the Frenchness replaced with British whimsy. It also reminds me a bit of the old Infogrames game Outcast in it's approach to free-roaming open world goodness and "stranger in a strange land" vibe. 

This game is brilliant - it takes all the elements I enjoyed from Subnautica, Elite and Mass Effect, and ramps them up a notch. Individual systems can be a bit janky, incomplete, or counter-intuitive, but put them all together and you've got the most audacious game I've ever played. £40 is a lot for a 4 year old game, but you get a lot of content which is ever-evolving. There's plenty of room for space-sims as far as I'm concerned (depending on personal preference) - Elite for the serious simulationists, the "X" series for empire builders and modders, Rebel Galaxy Outlaw for casuals, Star-Citizen for the perpetually optimistic, and No Man's Sky for the hopeful explorer.

I will include a tldr at the end for those that just want a brief review, but I'm first going to go over my thoughts about how the game was handled and the developers before reviewing the game itself.

I remember being one of those people that got very excited when the game was originally shown off at E3. I payed attention to most of the news that came out about the game and eagerly awaited its release. However, I didn't pre-order and instead waited for it to come out and to read some of the reviews. After the flood of negative reviews hit all across the internet, I ended up passing on the game in disappointment and forgetting about it for some time. 

I was surprised when I heard that the developers where still working on the game and adding new free content years after release; trying to improve the game and turn it into what everyone expected it to be on launch. This was about a year or so ago when I learned about the various improvements made, and I said to myself that if I felt that enough content was added, I would finally buy it. I ended up buying it during the steam summer sale for $30 (US), and I completed the main story and all of the side quests except for "Dreams of the Deep" before writing this review.

I am genuinely impressed by the work and dedication Hello Games has poured into this game. A game in which almost everyone denounced after launch, and nobody thought it would ever be improved or fixed. Hello Games have earned my respect for what they have done over the years following the release, and I want to say thank you. Thank you for your hard work and dedication towards making this game into something even better than what was expected, and I can't wait to see how this game will evolve in the years to come and what the next game will be from Hello Games.

Now onto my thoughts about the game itself. In short, it is a fairly solid game with some great ideas sprinkled throughout, but it is dragged down somewhat by some design decisions and bugs. Some of the aspects I thought were great was the language learning system, freighter/capital ships, various planet and space exploration mechanics, and some of the lore. I really like the fact that you have to learn alien languages before I can actually understand them. The main downfall of this is that you can only learn on word at a time and there are hundreds of words per species! I eventually gave up on learning a language after learning about 300 words for one species and realizing I might only be half way done learning it. This wouldn't have been a problem if you could do something like learn multiple words at once instead of one at a time, or require you to learn less words. I also really liked how freighters and capital ships acted as a mobile base with the ability to hire frigates to do expeditions. I ended up getting a class A capital ship with a fleet of frigates and constantly sending out expeditions to gather even more resources for me to hoard for story missions or sell instantly. The exploration was very good in the beginning but started declining after about 20 hours since I had discovered what I believe to be either all or most of the planet types (including the very strange/unique planets). It was nice to have a variety of places to explore ranging from inhabited and abandoned space stations/outposts, ancient ruins, and derelict freighters (in the most recent update as of the writing for this review). I also want to stress how I love the fact that you can explore basically anywhere which really makes you feel the scale of this game, and it make it feel like you are actually exploring even if it is only for a little while. However, due to the procedural generation nature of the game, many places start to look and act the same after some time and you stop exploring due to curiosity and start doing it purely for gaining resources. Lastly, I thought that they did some interesting this with the lore and background; specifically with the Korvax and Gek. Without spoiling anything, I want to say that their backgrounds and relationship was interesting and I can't recall off the top of my head another sci-fi story that had dome something like this. 

There are some significant flaws such as a general disappointment the rewards for the majority of the quests in the game. Most rewards don't feel big enough to compensate the amount of work that is required. The story is serviceable and predictable if you pay attention enough to the game environment and names of quests. The ending also feels somewhat anticlimactic, especially since the location used for the finally was also used in other parts of the game making it not feel like a unique and important place. The game isn't necessarily grindy, it just takes time to do some tasks such as finding specific resources. Lastly, the game is buggy in numerous places. I have had quests that got stuck in a reward loop giving me multiple copies of the same reward. My ship would do odd flips and spins when entering my capital ship sometimes. Textures not loading and/or clipping, and other smaller bugs popping their heads every now and again. None of them ever hurt my progress or caused crashes, they were just annoyances.

I will give this game a 3/5 for now with the potential to increase depending on how the game is updated in the future.

tldr;
3/5
It is a okay/good game that is worth about $30 (US). There are some flaws and bugs, but I generally feel that the positives outweigh the negatives. The game is still being improved and content is still being added, so this game can potentially become even better in the future.

Decent game, light-years ahead of where it first was on launch.

The core gameplay is fun, especially around early-mid game where you're just building up your arsenal of ship and multitool upgrades and exploring new environments. It can get repetitive much later on in the endgame though, unless you're someone who really likes filling out as much of the universe as you possibly can, which means you're going to be playing for a very, very long time. The in-game universe will likely never be fully explored due to the sheer number of stars and galaxies in it.

There are also some features in the game that seem unique, like the adjacency-directional upgrade amplification mechanic, the way you actually need to learn alien languages, and of course the scanning+uploading, but some of them aren't really used to their full potential in one way or another. For example, you can't unlock extra dialogue in said alien languages, you just understand more of what they're saying.

Still, Hello Games has shown a surprising amount of determination in making their flagship game good, instead of just taking the money and running or milking their product until it dies. I respect it. I believe that attitude will allow the game to grow to its full potential in due time.

I would write more but I'm kind of scouring a galaxy for the perfect ship designs though.

More Exocraft now, but still pitiful speeds un-modded. Checked my Mods folder, and of the mods were installed in 2018. :)

Downloaded updated mod for Exocraft speed -AFTER-  completing the quest-chain (on a water world) for the submarine. What a slog that was, when each of the locations required over 7-minutes of boring travel to reach them. And there were a few in the chain.

Back in the day, Creative mode freed me from using several mods which reduced the survival aspects of the game, which I've always felt were not my cup-o-tea.

But now I realize that I am in the trap caused by "Nothing has a cost, so everything is worthless"

i.e. came back to a save with 180+ hours, over 80-million credits, and 15k nanites. Decided I wasn't using both Exotic ships, and space station now has a scrap function - so I "melted" my least favorite exotic for scrap, and had 120-million worth of scrap placed in my inventory. I sold the scrap, and now have over 200-million credits.

Over 200-million credits - in Creative mode - where everything is free. 

My two fleets just returned from missions. One earning me 1.3-mil, and the other 900K. So there is another 2-million credits in my account... big whoop.

The flying around space and planets hasn't gotten old yet, but I've learned so many words that the knowledge stones are giving me: we, the, is... with every 5th one or so being more that 4-letters long.

I think about trying the normal mode, and then I'll have a storm come in, distort my vision and deplete my shields, and I'm reminded of why I'm not interested in running for safety every few minutes. And, of course the really 'valuable' stuff is on the planets with the worst weather... even in Creative, where there is no  reward for putting-up with the storms, just more -useless- money added to my account

I bought the game during the first half-price sale - following the initial release's scathing back-lash - when I figured I couldn't get hurt to bad for the price. That has been the case. The game still scratches the flying in a ship itch for me, and I enjoyed piecing-together the fragments of the three races history. But the solo-play aspects just haven't changed enough to keep me playing for more than a week or two, at this rate.
Reviews.128559:
I'm almost always against paying $60 for any game title - in fact, No Man's Sky was no exception at the time, as I scored it for half off. If I did it all over again, I would gladly pay full price for this game, and if you're a fan of exploration games and procedural generation, you likely won't regret doing so either.

I could sit here and regurgitate everything that the game offers, but I'll just give one reason: active developers. I bought the game about 9 months before I wrote this, and the game has come out with at least four massive content updates in that time that further add to the game's already limitless possibilities.

Simply put, No Man's Sky might be the best exploration game available on Steam. If you're looking for a way to kill a few hundred hours, pick it up.

Reviews.128622:
This game has made one hell of a recovery.
Everyone knows how this game was at launch, but as of this review there's so much new content that's been added that I would confidently say that this is one of my favorite space games.
The game's focus is far more on adventuring than crafting, which I really appreciate. I'm glad to have a break from endless crafting recipes. Every planet looks somewhat similar, but they still have lots of things on them to make going worthwhile. With an economy scanner installed on your ship, you can find a trade outpost from anywhere on a planet, and with a planetary chart you can find different facilities that contain exclusive crafting recipes for advanced tech and get coordinates to planetary depots you can raid for a great bounty of units.
Everything in the game, from wiring looms to entire spaceships, are, for good reason, very expensive. But the game makes up for this by providing lots of different ways to earn money. Do you want to farm plants to fabricate delicate and valuable electronic components, pirate freighters to steal their cargo, or go full Hitchhiker's Guide and survey planets for money, taking your "fair share" of the rare local curiosities to pawn off later?
This game is very solid in its current state, and I'm happy to say that Hello Games is still pouring countless updates into this game. This game did a serious 170* from horrendous to very, very good. I would very much suggest this game to anyone looking for a very solid space capitalism simulator or a great game that offers a break from microtransactions and lets you explore and build at your own pace.
9/10

Back in 2016 when the game was first released my initial thoughts were that this game is the biggest cash grab in the history of gaming community. However, 4 years have passed now and they redeemed themselves.

Pros:
-Vast (Almost Infinite) Open Universe to explore
-Large diversity of ships and tools
-Planetary biomes are well done and crafted
-Finding unique items are satisfactory and rewarding

Cones:
- It is a relaxed exploration game so might not be for everyone ( Meaning no crazy space fights or much danger at all)
- Ship controls are bit clunky ( especially with mouse and keyboard)
- Missions get repetitive overtime ( However, playing co-op makes it tolerable)
- Character Customization next to non-existent except color changes to your gear

Is It worth the price? Depends if you like exploration games even then there are much much better games on the almost the same category. 

Is it fun to play solo? Absolutely! ( Until you try coop then solo play becomes obsolete ).

Is the game going to develop further? Absolutely! Just by judging how far game has come since release I would say in couple years it might become fully grown online multiplayer RPG game with some FPS elements.

Overall, No Man's Sky is a fun game to explore and have fun with friends over your free time for couple hours. Nothing fancy or exciting. 

Score 7/10
