No Man's Sky, as it stands now, is quite fun and expansive despite its many flaws. The seemingly endless amount of planets and galaxies to explore give way to insurmountable possibilities and exploration. Though the game can be a lonesome, and at times, boring experience, there is still much to enjoy. However, I find that this game shines brightest when taking advantage of its recently updated multiplayer mode. Playing alone simply can't compete to playing with friends, though as I've mentioned it still stands on its own just fine. 

The game can be very buggy at times, some of the bugs even making quests more difficult than need be, but I usually find myself finding a way around these bugs. One other complaint I have is that the creature variety can often seem to be quite lacking, but there are times when I still find new creatures that blow my mind and/or disturb me, and it's quite an amazing feeling to experience for yourself and especially with friends despite it happening somewhat infrequently. One final complaint that I could think of would be with the interactions you have with other intellectual lifeforms. Whereas you can select dialogue, oftentimes it doesn't affect the outcome of the conversation. At times, you may need to help the conversation recipient make a decision or answer a question that may hold different outcomes depending on your response, but this doesn't happen as much as one-sided conversations do.

Whereas there are many ways in which this game falls short, there are even more ways in which it truly shines. The personalization in this game is quite nice, allowing you to name different planets, galaxies, creatures, plants, etcetera that you find during your journey, as well as allowing you to alter your character's appearance. Where this feature falls short, though, is with the inability to customize the appearance of your Starship as well as a few other things. You're also able to create a base of your own which can be an exhilarating experience, though it has its fair share of bugs and limitations, however, I found it overall pleasant.

I'm sure there are many things I haven't touched on simply because the game is so vast, but all in all, No Man's Sky has improved exponentially over the past few years, fixing many bugs and adding many features that help make the experience a much more personal and enjoyable experience. It has many drawbacks, so I can understand why some players may not enjoy the game, however, if exploration, material gathering, and Sci-Fi are what you're looking for, I'd recommend this one.

One of the greatest comeback stories of gaming. After bombing horribly on release due partly to over-hype, and partly to being very lacking in content and playability, Hello Games has stuck with this (very) rough gem through years, and gradually turned it into not just a good, but a very damn good game.

The game is still - first and foremost - about exploration, and it's main gameplay mechanism is - still - grinding for resources to craft ever more advanced items (and bases now), but it also has a lot of other content now. Still if you either hate exploration games, or cannot set aside grinding to "win" a game and just enjoy it for a while, you might find NMS less than ideally suited to your tastes.

But for everyone else it is highly, highly recommended. You can often find it for 50% off (usually when a new amazing patch lands), and at that price this should be an instant buy for anyone not in the group previously mentioned.

There's great parts of this game. Exploration and discovery, both of the worlds and the tools available to you. The music, and the sombre, meditative mood it helped to create. The hints of a strange, ambitious story.

For me, the bad outweighed the good. That ambitious story was unsatisfying, poorly paced, and had to be pursued through buggy quests and ordering issues. All the critics after launch kept me from getting this game, but they've had a ton of updates since release and they've given them for free.  No DLC in this game which I LOVE.  It was on Steam sale this week for $30 and I'm glad I bought it.  

I'm also glad I waited.  Reading through the release notes for the updates I realize there have been so many quality of life improvements to the game that I don't think I would have liked the original.  You can equip tech to your starship and freighter to transfer cargo at a distance for instance.  Inventory management is a pain before you get all your upgrades anyway, this really helped.

I started the game without really reading anything about it and it was not too hard to figure out what was happening.  It was really cool trying to figure out how to stay alive as I repaired my ship.  After you get to the Nexus which won't be too far into playing go ahead and watch a starter video or two to learn more about the gameplay though, there are tips that just make life easier.

Don't worry too much about inventory management would be my biggest tip.  Keep the basic elements you need to keep your suit and ship functioning and get rid of the rest.  Don't feel too bad about destroying anything else.  Get drop pod coordinates or visit new stations to get suit inventory upgrades.  Get navigation data from stations and buildings (little orange or blue cubes) and use your signal booster to find distress signals and you can claim new ships for free and decommission them on stations to get storage upgrades for your main ship.

And explore the options in the quick menu (hold X).  You can have up to three multitools and swap them out, and you can summon your ship as long as it has launch fuel, and pick a different ship if you have more than one.  Follow the quests for a while, your base research stations will teach you some plans for free.
Reviews.128902:
No Man's Sky is unique. 

It's too casual and relaxed to consider it a serious space fighter game a la Elite:Dangerous. It could be an exploration game with light story elements and light RPG elements. You'll spaceship shoot bad guys and FPS shoot floating robots. Also maybe animals, if you're into that. And rocks and plants and stuff.

It's super grindy. The main grinds (build this tech) have sub-grinds (gather mats to build components). Once you get good at grinding you'll find new ways to grind things you didn't know existed whilst getting faster at regular grinding, and at some point if you stick with it you'll look at the old things you used to gather and see that you don't have to collect them anymore.

There's also a lot of traveling. Also, lots of inventory management. If you really like virtually transporting images of widgets to or from your personal inventory to or from your ship inventory or to or from your freighter inventory then this game should be the best game ever.

Plus, there's scanning stuff. Think of that as gathering data on stuff that somehow pays out tiny chunks of money. I short shrifted the traveling element, which for space could be described as 'colorful loading screens you can manipulate periodically.' You can also walk places and ride vehicles places. You can also just walk or drive no specific place just to see what's there or say you did. That's an option here, too.

This stuff all melds great into a multi-tiered achievement field that rewards you for doing all of those grinds. It's possibly one big reputation grind on top of separate doing stuff grinds that all have sub-grinds (gathering this, shooting that, feeding this, discovering that, etc). I'm too tired right now to really extrapolate all the grinds.

It's got a story that I've yet to complete after 167 hours and for the life of me I'd struggle to even suggest to you what it's about. Like, there's this entity that's either good or evil or neither that does - maybe did? - something and you're this traveler who periodically unravels aspects of that or those action(s) in order to give all that grinding you did purpose. Oh, and there are or were other NPC travelers who the game would have you believe did some of this before or after you, depending on unspecific time paradoxes. It seems fair that other entities should have to go through all that. Plus, if you prefer, you could just try to get to the center of the universe. I recommend that for all of the loading screen fans.

I forgot to mention the three main alien types you meet in the game each only tell you one word of their entire vocabulary at a time, and only if you ask them to. They appear to know hundreds of words each. I think there are ways to increase your ability to learn with science if you're willing to grind out the ways to learn them. The more vocabulary you learn the better your odds at solving certain puzzles. I don't know what gaming itch this scratches, but I've scratched it. This really starts to clarify how I've logged so many hours in this title.

So why do I recommend all this? Well, like I said at the jump, it's unique. I've enjoyed figuring out what all to do with all the tools at my disposal in order to make them into tools I've see in my travels or in advertisements for the game. I've yet to get anywhere close to endgame content and 1) I've been at it for a while and 2) I'm just starting to, so the effort is paying off. Also, lots of it can be skipped if you know other benevolent people who play the game or are willing to deep dive wiki pages.

The game is colorful, it's relaxing, it's not overly complex or stressful. It trickles in micro-rewards that keep me going toward moderate rewards. I'm not the type of player who'd ever try to finish this in one sitting (if that's possible) - but it's a decent game to check in on from time to time to unlock more puzzle pieces. Just seeing the art fly past at high speeds is nice. And, if you're vain, you can leave your mark by being the first to see things - and you can name them after yourself, your friends, your enemies, whatever. I like not knowing what's coming and figuring out the puzzles without much input from the internet. Plus there's co-op, something I've never tried here.

So if you want to pretend like you're a space person doing mildly space-like things basically over and over again while some sort of story unfolds around you and you visit colorful places you can poke around in to achieve ambiguous goals, I can think of no better title that tried to stuff all of that in to one game over the span of something like a decade than No Man's Sky.

I've been playing this off and on for at least several months now, and I like the game so much that I would feel a little bad if I didn't write a review. For me, it's a great game for zoning out and forgetting about the actual world. I have a decent graphics card and a fairly large monitor, and the game feels incredibly immersive and often inspires awe with scenes that make me glad that the game has a photo mode. There's plenty of content to go through, but most of it is optional and can be saved for later if you don't feel like doing it. I played for several dozen hours before finishing off one of the main story quests and had a great time. If a long and complex story is a major thing that you're looking for, this probably isn't the game for you; but there is a huge number of small lore details scattered around the universe in places like ancient relics, abandoned buildings, and conversations with aliens and occasional other travelers. It's up to you to piece them together since quests only cover some of it.

The main focus of the game is exploration, and most players should get many hours out of that before exploration starts to lose some of its luster. But rare themed "glitch" planets can briefly revive a lot of excitement even after things get stale. And it took a long time for exploration to get stale for me because there were so many other things in the game to do (like upgrading storage and equipment or taking on missions or learning alien languages or learning new crafting recipes or building bases). There's so much that can be done at any time that it's easy to lose track or get distracted. Thankfully, quests and missions are saved in a tab in the menu, so they can be selected to help remember what you're supposed to do for them and to pin them to the HUD. And finding the quest you want in the menu is sometimes necessary because taking on new quests shifts the HUD focus to the new one.

A major flaw of the game is that it has a good deal of bugs. Most are visual (especially on older hardware) and not game breaking, but I've had some pretty annoying ones happen in older versions, especially when I had an older computer with a very old processor and a case that didn't have enough airflow to adequately cool my graphics card (so maybe my fault?). They're working on fixing bugs over time, but it seems like there will always be some. Thankfully, existence of bugs kind of make sense in the game's universe, and one that was frequently frustrating during multiplayer was fixed in the most recent patch. There is more room for improvement, but I appreciate the improvements they've made.

I read that the game dramatically underdelivered at launch, but the version I played is excellent. I want to thank the developers for all of the free content/updates that they have added and continue to add. No Man's Sky's development and expansion over time is the ultimate video game comeback story.

Reviews.128947:
No Man's Sky is a good attempt at reaching for everything in a genre that games are usually locked into one or two aspects. It does a good job at making things like (Space Combat, Ground Combat, Exploration, "Vague Storytelling", and Space Simulation) Simple for a larger audience. Now simple doesn't mean bad especially if the amount of simple things are put together to make a larger more complex story or game. What seems like a game of resource gathering, vague storytelling, and alien races turns into a narrative driven by the player, Yes a story exists however this story is left broad for a reason. Yes alien races do exist (However in smaller numbers then what is typical for other games of the genre) They exist to ping off the character and narrative that the player makes, By making the species of aliens so keenly fit into certain niches of the genre you will be naturally drawn to one or another. This applies to exploration as well, while some people might find a planet full of mushrooms and toxic spores interesting and might even adapt their character to live on them. I do not however No Man's Sky has allowed this to happen for a reason. You may be stuck in or on areas that seem horrible and that may hurt your eyes or brain to look at however this makes it so much sweeter when you finally find a place that you can call your own for one reason or another and makes the journey before (though some of it may be rough and horrible) feel a lot more worth it. There are some aspects that are a little too easy (what comes to mind is how the player gets their first "Frigate" or how me as someone who primarily plays Elite: Dangerous would call it a Fleet Carrier) these will hurt the experience for people that are either older or more used to the genre. Overall I have concluded at least in the non spoiler part of my review that if the art style of No Man's Sky was a little less cartoonish and the game was a little less casual (This is my personal preference of course) I would call it the best space game I have ever played. However due to the nature of the game and what platforms and audience it was made for it is prone to at times feeling like you are basically riding a railroad track disguised as a space game. 7/10 (Check below for spoiler section and new rating based on these facts)


(Potential Spoilers Ahead)


No Man's Sky's narrative is interesting however it falls short in the fact that everything is very heavy handed. Your character professes in potentially the last couple of story missions "I AM A SIMULATED ENTITY" despite player input saying they "Could be real" or something similar. Also the fact that everything is a simulation is smacked in your face as soon as the opening of the game (not subtly either) I understand the game was made for younger audiences however this "story" or aspect of the game had me just wanting to finish it so I could go make a cool underwater base and get an alien like space ship. The story drags in places and your decisions in the end don't really matter (These being the fates of two (potentially three?) fellow "Travelers" you meet along your journey one who is named =Null=. Very subtle indeed) The potential narrative given by "Haunted Terminals" is never played on since this is a simulation. It could very well be that other entities made this as a sort of game for others to find. The only plot I could find interesting was self (and maybe a bit by the game) the flying robots IE: sentinels appear out of no where sometimes when you are doing things in the game, This lead me to believe (After the "SIMULATION" theory was confirmed) that these things could be anti viruses and that the "simulation" that we live in was made as a sort of show of computing power or show of a computer's understanding of life (Specifically an AI's understanding of life) however where this falls flat is the fact that later down the road you learn that ATLAS the main focus of the story has been repeating the same cycle for 16 minutes of its shutdown period... it has retreaded inside itself and is making infinite realities in itself to figure out what is wrong and what it can do to fix it before it is shut down. However the problem may be that the AI sees life so simple that three alien races can be put into cliches (Scientist, Merchants, Warriors). I do see that the AI could of been exposed to genocide (IE WW2 or such) while being given info to simulate reality in its own experience, and this would explain the first "simulation" and the "Error" that the creator of the AI saw. However this doesn't make the game less bland since it (at least in my 110 hours of the game) never explains this. 

Overall the Story doesn't need to be in the game it adds a lot to think about, However it forces a wedge between what could of potentially been greatness and early reviews (though unfair in some degrees) reflect this... It seems the story was really thrown in at the last minute to explain something that didn't need explanation.

Overall Score 8/10 (Though the story didn't add anything to an average player and may even confuse them greatly, It got me thinking and that makes it decent however the way these missions were executed especially the last "official" mission was very well done)

(edited for spelling mistakes)

Thank you for reading!

Reviews.129079:
It might be better, but it's still a pointless game.

It's "procedurally generated" which means once you've spent a couple of hours flying around checking stuff out, you've practically, if not literally, seen it all. 
There's no point in having trillions of permutations if there's no actual difference between the planets and places you visit. 

There are loads of different space stations that look different from one another, yet they're identical with the exception of a few assets moved around and the people inside have random appearances within the four races that are there.
The buildings and ruins you can find are all the same ten or so templates, again with small differences. 
The planets themselves can look very distinct from one another and very wildly, but in practice it's all the same; You point a beam at a rock or a tree and you get a generic resource plus maybe a slightly rarer one occasionally. 
The animals come in three varieties: Ground passive, ground hostile and flying passive. They look wildly different from one another, but all you can do with them is shoot, feed or look at them. 

The base building is interesting, but the assignable posts give you bleak and depressing stories.

Speaking of stories, everyone and everything you interact with is negative in some way, hopeless, nihilistic, obsessed with greed or war and it takes hours of clicking through slow dialogue boxes to learn words so that you can even understand them in the first place, which is largely pointless because why bother listening to people that are all sad or depressing in some way?

The gameplay itself is boring and unrewarding.
The game will insist you do mundane tasks constantly while also not actually telling you anything about how to make the many millions it takes from upgrading to a ship that has halfway decent inventory space. Even if you do figure out how to make a lot, you can't spend it unless you randomly come across the ship or freighter you want. 

There's no sense of progression or reward, you just grind through boring and repetitive tasks and then hopefully come across what you think looks nice and even then it's more about the amount of slots you get and how many upgrades you can cram in to get some feeling of improvement on your stats. 

The game is an overpriced novelty with very few redeeming qualities. Also it runs kind of poorly considering its age. 
You want a grindy game where you set your own goals and work to see actual results? Get Ark instead.

This is the "best worst game ever". It's got a lot of issues but it's so, so fun. Don't expect a simulator, it's very arcade-y but it's excellent at it.

Pros: Gorgeous graphics. satisfying and addictive exploration, tons of new content and features added regularly, fun multiplayer.

Cons: very unpolished with pervasive bugs (including multiplayer), all space stations are identical, gibberish story and repetitive quests, interchangeable NPCs, repetitive world generation, heavy emphasis on inventory management, worthless maps and navigation, heavy reliance on wikis and other external resources.

VR is a token effort but ultimately worthless, really just couch play and not roomscale since the interface doesn't turn and you can't move from the center, but the worst dealbreaker is the abysmal the motion controls on the spaceship. Really wish they'd improve this because it makes the multiplayer better but at this point I just play on a screen.

Steam link streaming also has some bugs that make spaceflight difficult, but you can get some basic tasks done remotely.

I...used to hate you. 

Even seeing you mentioned, anywhere on the interwebs would annoy me. 

Some might say the hate was justified, after the fustercluck that your game was, but then, you started to work on it, adding new things over time, repairing the admittedly severe damage you'd done to the potential relationship you'd have with people who bought into the stuff you'd said in the beginning. Both figuratively and literally.  Now look at you, you're a whole lot of fun, with a lot of stuff to do and see. 

Wanna build a base, a compound, a whole freakin' town? You can do that! 
Wanna go rummage around ancient ruins for treasure/valuables? Go for it!
Wanna own your own freighter and supporting ships, while being able to send a selection of the latter on missions, to acquire goods? Sounds like a plan! 
Wanna go explore the mysteries of the NMS universe? That's definitely an option!
Perhaps you fancy going out to look for a new ship to zoom around in, something with a little more zing than your current space bucket? The variety will keep you going!
Maybe you want to explore the depths of some backwater planet, in your little submersible? Why not! 

Or.....perhaps you'd like to board and salvage the contents of a cold, dark, dangerous,  abandoned freighter, stripping it of the valuables it holds, in order to maybe make a nice little profit? Now you can

No Man's Sky is a one trick pony really, unless you change the pony with mods. And even then, since there are so little mods, it gets boring. I had a good run with the game. I have played 415 hours. I started with a normal character, unmodded. I got bored about 200 hours in and restarted with mods. Then I got bored again and wanted something harder so I decided to do perma death. I have gotten most of the achievements while playing perma but that burned out too. The latest content release is Desolation. I thought it was neat for anyone into the capitol ship game play, it doesn't have anything there to make me want to play again.

If you have never played it, this is worthy of your time. Do not make multiple characters. I suggest playing on the hardest diff you can stomach and throwing some mods in at the very start for planet generation. Make your one play your only play. That way the game stays fresh and you will be 'done' right around the time you get bored.

So why did I get bored? The game uses random generation for most content in the game. However, the 'random' pool is very, very small. All the animals look like clones after the first 20 or so planets. Most planets repeat some plants and crystals over and over killing out the idea you are in a random universe of unique planets. Honestly if the game just had a ton more variety it would help, but it will never fix it entirely. The human brain is really good at picking out patterns. And once it has...it gets bored. Things become predictable.

That's my take. Hope it helps somebody. :)

Game is continually being updated and expanded, devs are always actively looking for things to fix or improve, and I have yet to see a major update which did not positively contribute to the quality of the game in some meaningful way.

Biggest criticism right now is that ship handling and space flight overall is really really lame. Controls are loose and sloppy with not a lot of depth to combat, weapon use, in-ship control systems, etc. Not saying we need another Elite:Dangerous here but could we maybe have something at least as engaging as Everspace?  Would love to see an overhaul of this aspect of the game someday.

The other big glaring problem is the multiplayer, specifically base building. There is no way for a group of friends to share ownership of one base and all contribute to it and benefit from it equally.

All you can do is "visit" each other's bases and even with full permissions granted by the owner, you can only build/modify the base when the owner is also online. More than anything I would like to see the kind of shared ownership/building that you have in games like Minecraft, where bases become an ongoing persistent area of group involvement where friends create something together and any member of a base can build/modify/access the shared inventory regardless of who else is signed into the game. This isn't really possible right now, and it's a shame. I hope this will be addressed someday. Same thing with freighters: cool in concept but not so great in multiplayer.

We need shared freighters that a small group of friends can all crew and own together, not the system we have now where you can just dock and visit each other's freighters but not do anything of consequence while there. I want to dock at a friend's freighter and help gather supplies for it, add to its inventory, build facilities inside, plot routes, etc; and when I sign off I want my friend to be able to fly to a new location and when I sign on again I want to still be in that same freighter in its new location. Not a thing right now. I hope it's possible and I hope it will happen eventually.

Overall though it's a wonderful experience and if you don't care about the multiplayer, there really aren't many glaring flaws here.

Now, in No Man's Sky everything is so snappy! It motivates me to do everything I described I don't wanna do in Elite Dangerous.

So much potential in this game but I really can't recommend it having just had it crash on me AGAIN and waste an hour or so of base building and collecting resources. This has probably happened to me a dozen times now. The game really needs an auto-saving feature since it is so unreliable.

The game is riddled with annoying glitches like being teleported to the surface for no reason when you are base-building underground. Many pieces of base technology are incompatable with the vast majority of building components i.e. wood, metal or concrete structures. Electro-magnetic generators which need to be placed in a specific (like, down to a square foot) place to generate any electricity, for some reason, often can't locate anywhere suitable nearby, or direct you to a location which is too distant from your base or is completely unaccessable. There are ground and aquatic base components, but they are incompatable with each other so there is no way to connect a land base to an aquatic base. You can build a base on your freighter, but if you then upgrade your freighter your base is lost, which make sense, but basically means there is no point building anything on your freighter until you reach the late game and buy the best freighter, which costs, I think, something like 125 million in space currency and spawns randomly. I've just reached this point after 150 hours on the game.

You're inventory is initially tiny and at the start you have no storage space so you are constantly having to manage your inventory and throw things away to make room for more valuable things, or you will miss out on them completely because if you mine something, or the game throws a random event at you that you couldn't have predicted which gives you something, and your inventory is full, the item or resources are lost.

Missions can be glitchey too, you may complete an objective but the mission doesn't register it as completed. You may start a mission with a friend online but for some reason the mission fails to load for them. In one case I joined a friend with a mission to build a base but was unable to do anything to contribute to it so he had to do it all. The mission which randomly pops up occasionally to collect a bounty on a nearby starship prevents you from landing on your frigates until you go and do it.

While the game itself is good fun for the most part, it's also a little disappointing how unlike space the NMS universe is. In every system you visit the planets are crowded closely together when they should really be distant dots on the night sky. The closeness of the planets means at least one usually obscures another completely. You might even just stumble upon a little black hole while flying between them, which is especially underwhelming - black holes should be gigantic and beautiful, with a bright accretion disc and a dangerous magnetic pull, not popping up unexpectedly in the middle of solar systems without anyone noticing and without having any effect at all on the extremely nearby planets. Every planet is rocky and habitable, indeed most have some form for flora and fauna, there are no gas giants like Saturn or Jupiter anywhere. Virtually every planet is guarded by irritating aggressive robots that don't let you collect resources and spawn endlessly if you fight them. There is a reasonable amount of variety, but all planets fit into about half a dozen categories (hot, cold, radioactive, acidic, no atmosphere, and one or two weird kinds of artificial looking planets) and you will find flora and fauna on various different planets that look exactly the same, but scan as being different species - you will find the exact same 3 models on virtually every planet for dangerous plants - a sort of venus fly trap, a whip-like plant and a plant that explodes toxins into the air).

Although you are hailed as some kind of uniquely blessed explorer, in fact every system seems to already be claimed by one of the three main alien species you will encounter, and contains pirates and freighters and random events like ship wreckage. Every planet already contains outposts, crashed spaceships, those irritating robots, and ancient ruins, but despite the fact they are everywhere, you will never find a city full of aliens. Space stations are the busiest places you will find, where there are perhaps a couple dozen NPCs, but a good few of them are hidden away in rooms you will rarely enter.

As it is I'm unsatisfied with this game, and I got the game on sale for about £20.00, if I had paid full price I'd be pretty angry. If the game is optomised a lot more so that it runs more smoothly and coolly, stops crashing, and the numerous bugs and glitches are ironed out, I would be more than satisfied with this game the way it has been designed. If it had been designed to be a little more like real space as well, I'd have been delighted with it.

Before anything, i bought and played the game at launch.
I have seen it grow over all the major updates, and have returned a couple of times since then.

To make it clear, i have been rooting for this game since before it was released, and i'm still rooting for it.
Part of me is happy that Hello Games has invested so much into making new content for it, and i have to acknowledge the fact that it has now turned into a full-fledged space exploration game.

No Man's Sky has clearly gone a long way.

And this is why it really tears me apart, after all these years of waiting for the "redemption", that i now have to leave a negative evaluation here.

I want to play NMS. I want to like it, and enjoy it. But i can't.
The reason for this is very simple : The game is bugged to an extent that you wouldn't even imagine.

You remember how people always refer to Bethesda as "the studio who releases buggy games" ? Well, i've played my share of Bethesda games and i've never experienced something as buggy as NMS so far.

The game is extremely fun, but it's clogged with bugs, literally EVERYWHERE. Every 10 minutes, just as you start getting immersed in the incredible universe that is NMS, you get yet another bug that comes slapping you in the face, and ruins the experience.

Here is a non-exhaustive list of what i have experienced in ONLY 2 DAYS (count less than 10 hours) of playing the last update (Beyond - Exomech) :
- Enemies teleporting into the ground and shooting you
- Quests not counting completed objectives (which means that you can't finish them without starting over)
- Entering an empty anomaly while in a multiplayer session (need to leave and rejoin the session)
- Ship landing into the ground (need to restart the game)
- Getting teleported at a random timing by the Nexus, back to the system where you originally started a mission that required you to change system
- LOSING YOUR BASE AND FLEET WHEN TELEPORTING WITH THE NEXUS
- ...

These bugs happened repeatedly, and for me the last one was the nail in the coffin.
I had my fleet and my base since the Atlas Rises ~ Next update, so as you can imagine this was a big no-no for me.

The worst part in all this is that, after looking all these bugs up, i realized that people had already reported them since YEARS ago. AND THEY STILL HAVEN'T BEEN FIXED !!
HELLO ! A BUG THAT MAKES YOU LOSE YOUR BASE AND FLEET HAS BEEN AROUND FOR YEARS ! HELLO !

I mean, come on ! Don't they have any kind of QA process at Hello Games ? How do these broken updates even get released in such an unacceptable state ? And HOW DO THEY LEAVE THESE BUGS UNADDRESSED FOR YEARS ??

As i said, i want to play NMS. I want to play it so bad. But who knows what's next ? If players can lose their fleet and base over a stupid teleport, and Hello Games doesn't care enough to fix that, who knows what's next ?
I'm sorry, but this is it for me.
I didn't leave a bad review on release, despite the lies and the barebones-state the game was in.
I didn't leave a bad review after that, despite the lack of communication from Hello Games, or despite the fact that the content we were given was still not enough to make NMS a good game.

I supported this game since the beginning, but if this is what i get after waiting for 4 years, then i have to say i can't cheer for Hello Games anymore.
The bugged state that NMS is in is plainly unacceptable. I have played MANY games in early-access that were in a better state than this.

Sorry to demistify the whole "redemption" thing that everyone is cheering about.

Has NMS gone a long way in terms of content ? Yes it has.
Is it playable ? No.

Please do not buy this and encourage Hello Games to keep the same behavior.

After playing around 60 hours, I have a bit more to say about this game.

I found this game to be quite time-absorbing to say the least, given these 60 hours have been accrued over the last 2-3 months only. With the many updates this has gotten, and is still getting, which have continually improved and added new content to this game, the scene and gameplay is kept relatively fresh and new. Although resource gathering can be a bit of a grind, no let's say a hell of a grind if you want to get everything, the places you can explore and the many planets with varied environments, flora and fauna more than make up for it. 

You can easily get by in the game without an S-class Venator max slot freighter, but hell, why not grind 4-6 hours or more to get 178 million units, and then another 1-10 hours (based on luck) to get the design and the class that you want. IDK if it was worth it, but I was hella satisfied and still am with the freighter I have. 

Want some cool spaceships? You get them alright, but let's just say that the chances of finding one are pretty low, dependent on type of system and like where u look. Pretty hard to find a perfect ship, there isnt really one, but you are really spoilt for choice. I mean perhaps the hours of searching for a couple of s class haulers or explorers may put some people off, but honestly you can get by without one. 

Lastly, the freedom in this game is amazing. Want to complete the storyline, you can. Want to wander off in the opposite direction to the storyline, you also can. Want to never finish the story and settle down with your tamed rideable pets, sure why not? Want to be a nomad and continually explore the stars, that is an option. 
You can basically play this game however you like, and at whatever pace you like.

There is a multiplayer aspect to this, which is quite peaceful I would say. There is no hard competition, no blowing up other people's bases, just relatively peaceful coexistence with other players, or that is at least what I have experienced, and finding friends is relatively easy.

In terms of modding, the game is pretty nice in terms of the developers accepting mods, the general rule is just to not ruin other player's gameplay. Tired of the grind, there is creative mode or some mods which can help you. 

Basically, you have a massive universe, and can play however you want. 

That is why I love this game, and will continue to play for the foreseeable future.

Waited 3 years to give this a shot. I let the dust settle down and extreme opinions of weirdly offended players fade away, all updates rolled out and stabilized. Seems like a good time to try NMS. Well, I played for less than two hours so i'll ask for a refund. NMS is definitely not for me. Here I will outline why and maybe it helps someone make a decision.

The highest gameplay level (the thing you do on a moment-to-moment basis) is very boring. You do 3 things:
1. Walk around and collect resources by clicking on things
2. Fly on your spaceship.
3. navigate menus and menus and more menus

Apart for item 3, writing it out like this makes it sound promising: walking on alien planets and flying on a spaceship? sign me up! But the implementation falls flat. The first two items are trivial. Walking around is understandably trivial but flying a spaceship should not be trivial, come on. That's such a wasted opportunity to introduce interesting gameplay mechanics and challenges. Unfortunately it's the most trivial aspect of the game. You point and the ship goes. Zero regards for physics, which I understand is a matter of opinion, but at least that would add challenge to the game. Acquiring orbit, matching velocities, docking, landing etc. These things are rewarding to master, add a dose of challenge and real risk, which in turn would validate resource gathering for repairing or improving maneuverability. These things could be acquired without realism too, as proved by many spaceship games, but it needs to be much more than point and go.

As is, the only motivation given by direct gameplay to gather resources is to... gather more resources. The storyline tries to motivate that by giving you a trail to follow. Signals left behind by someone or something. Interesting, but that doesn't hold the game on its own.

The third item, menu navigation, needs to be included in such a list because there is so much of it! And it's clumsy as hell too. It's just such a boring thing to be doing in a game that advertises itself as a space exploration game.

And without challenge in flying, the exploration game mode is a hard sell too. It's a glorified atlas of a procedural universe. For that purpose one could do better with Space Engine, in my opinion.

None of this makes the game inherently bad, just not for me. If you are the kind of person who enjoys navigating menus to craft things that can be used to craft more things, give NMS a chance. I don't mean it sarcastically, it just sounds like it because I really don't like doing these things! Who the hell likes it? I feel I'm being too kind with the first sentence of this paragraph which smells a lot like a "it's not you it's me" routine. Maybe it is you, NMS. Maybe it is you.

TL:DR - the game doesn't support a traditional 'joystick,' and certainly not a HOTAS. On top of that, you occasionally have to completely reinstall the game because reasons.

When No Many's Sky was released, it fell short of the hype.  That has certainly dramatically improved.  But even though it fell short, I enjoyed the game.  It did not advertise nor support using a traditional Joystick.  It worked with the Xbox 360 controller only.  Personally, I do not enjoy using a gamepad or mouse to 'fly' a space ship.  So I used x360ce to emulate the Xbox360 controller.  And then I used my Logitech or Thrustmaster to control the ship.

But then along came the BEYOND update.  And Hello Games made the decision to integrate with Steam BIg Picture.  That bricked x360ce, and so the game is back to just supporting a mouse or a gamepad.  Oh, sure, you can map a generic controller in Steam Big Picture.  But the problem is, to map a generic controller as a 360 or steam controller, it has to have at least as many buttons as the one you're emulating.  Therefore, neither my joystick nor HOTAS will work anymore.

For this reason I can't recommend this game.

If you find a workaround, then great!  The core game is fun.  There is plenty to do (despite some reviews.)

Reviews.152331:
I've seen a lot of posts recently about NO MANS SKY... positive, negative, inquisitive, and comparative. I wanted to offer my experience as someone who has spent hundreds of hours watching the universe be developed over the last few years (first on console, then across two PC builds to keep up with the development) by Hello games. I actually got so immersed into it at one point that I began writing my own lore stories to accompany my gameplay.

Yeah, I'm that type of nerd.

There are often comparisons to other space-type games when talking about NMS. I won't plug them in this review, but I'm sure you know the top contenders. Each of them offers something unique within the genre - which attributes to their success with a general audience, as well as a niche crowd. When you load up one, don't expect all the gameplay offered in the others.

NO MANS SKY is basically a Walking Simulator Cocktail; it's made like this:

Walking Simulator Base
+ 2 parts spacecraft piloting
+ 1 part collecting/crafting
+ 1 part base building
Garnish with PvE Survival

If you expect it to taste any different, you may be disappointed.

What NMS offers that the other contenders don't is the base of the game - walking simulation. Putting your feet on the ground of a procedurally generated planet that noone has ever laid eyes on before [even in VR if you want] - and not just any planet... one of 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 full-scale unique planets that were generated at the big bang (or server boot, whichever).

Name another game that offers that.

The technical marvel contained within that reality alone is astonishing. Then to do it with no load screens? ASTONISHING. Then to go on to accomplish things like tieing every unique simulation of the game running on peoples PCs together into one grand tapestry of first-come-first-discovered exploration... in full crossplatform coop with your friends... some using VR if they want.

Mind: Explodinated.

It's possible I'm wrong though - I often see comments writing all of that off because "the game is boring - it's like the same 5 planet types over and over. Dice roll. Meh."

This is actually a point I kind of agree with, although the variety has been enough for me honestly to not strike as monotonous. Regardless, what's important to remember is that over the last 4 years they have released 10 major developmental updates (DLCs) totally free:

FOUNDATIONS - game optimization, base building overhaul
PATHFINDER - vehicles, base sharing, ship customization
ATLAS RISES - storyline, procedural missions, economy, trade
NEXT - graphics overhaul, full multiplayer, unlimited base building, freighters
THE ABYSS - underwater overhaul, 5x more variety, sea creature AI
VISIONS - new biomes, more diversity, new fauna/flora, archaeology
BEYOND - full VR implemented, multiplayer expanded, NPC overhaul
SYNTHESIS - *community frequently requested* feature update, terrain editing
LIVING SHIP - sentient spaceship you keep as a pet and then pilot when it's old enough
EXO MECH - they added a Mech... it's amazing... wait, you need to know more?

This is called development. Complaining about an early access game not offering something you want is like complaining that an artist has only used 7 of the 10 colors on thier palette. BE PATIENT. Some people like to watch the artist paint - some people like to buy the finished painting. We know who you are.

Clearly - Hello Games isn't finished. The only question that sits unanswered is "What's going to be in the next update?" which has me dreaming that NMS will eventually offer an all encompassing experience when they're finished. I think you'd be foolish to tune out now.

//COPPER PIXEL

Reviews.155081:
Developers, pay close attention to this one. 

There have been countless times a game has come out to poor reception. Big promises that end up being broken promises. Hello Games' No Man's Sky is one of those games. 

This was a game to follow when it was first announced. The journey seemed amazing from conception to release. And that is when that journey turned into a nightmare. The release was terrible. Not one, not two, but many things promised ended up missing. And on top of that, it was just a buggy mess. So what is the developer to do? Well, in the case of many other developers, the first thing you do is go straight to damage control. "Ooops. We dun goofed. We'll fix that!" "Send us your crash reports" "Sorry". 

Yeah. We're used to that by now. Granted, some developers do the damage control thing and still manage to eventually pump out a decent product in the long run. But some just don't. Hello Games went a different and more risky approach. They shut their mouths. Some would say they went into hiding. And at the beginning, that may have been true. We may never know. But the bottom line is, They shut their mouths, so they could get busy working. They never gave up on us. Secretly behind closed doors they were actually working on the game, and eventually we got some updates. It was not perfect. But we got updates. And then more updates. And more. And major expansion caliber updates. Stuff that other developers would gladly have charged money for. But we got them. For free. And the train is not stopping. This is not just a redemption story for a developer that was once for a time loathed. This is also a showcase of how a developer is continuing to make their product better and better, and not asking for a red cent extra beyond the base price of the game. New content update after new content update. the game has grown exponentially. And for a game that already by definition is massive, that is a wonderful thing. From VR updates to new story content to entire new dynamics on how and what to explore, the game just keeps getting better and better. 

The game is not perfect yet. But it is more than what we asked for at launch by a huge margin. And Hello Games, good job. Damn good job. But word of advice? If you decide to ever make a new game? And I hope you do. Just make sure to save some of the ambitious details and keep them under wraps until they are baked into the game! Just give us the basic notes, and wow us later.

[h1]If you enjoy World of Warcraft-style inventory management and have zero expectations. No Man's Sky is the perfect game for you.[/h1]

If I was ten years younger I would have thought No Man's Sky to be brilliant and inspiring, but I find almost every aspect of it disappointing as-is. Yes, there's a lot to do, but the entirety of the game is basically a collection of minigames and an endless - and I mean truly endless - amount of inventory micromanagement. I've wasted so much time and grown so anxious about what to delete to make room for things like copper that I simply can't enjoy the game past a certain point. 

The game aspires to be a stress-free exploration title. It really isn't for a few reasons, the most important being that you can easily botch an entire expedition or strand yourself by not bringing the right materials from the right place. Subnautica has some of these issues - it's called a failure cascade - but nothing nearing No Man's Sky level of derangement. To truly explore you need to carry with you the building blocks of all your equipment, or stow them in your ship which is usually full of ship-related materials like Gold, Silver, Platinum, etc. Space mined stuff. 

If they simply increased the stack size of these items or gave you the in-inventory crafting system that almost every other game on the planet has, you'd be free of these issues. I lose an inventory slot just to carry a smelter so I can combine dust motes so I can gain and inventory slot. I have to do this all the time just to keep slots clear because things like opening containers or even exploring a wreck fills your open slots with slime items or rusted scraps. To delete these items you need to click your controller stick, which is quite literally the easiest way to kill your controller. In the 110 hours I have on No Man's Sky (and whatever I spent on AC:Odyssey) I've broken two xbox controllers by the sheer amount of stick clicking required to do actions. 

The patches are frequently referred to on the forum as "nothing" because the things they often add are obtuse or hidden behind systems that are entirely unexplained. For example, I still have absolutely no idea how to make the ground vehicles and I only recently stumbled upon water travel, which was hidden behind some quests to explore something unrelated. On that note, the writing of the game itself tries extremely hard to be vague and mysterious but ends up conveying absolutely nothing at all. The story - if you could call it a story - is a meandering tale of nonsense that, like everything else, sets you up for disappointment if you even follow the bread crumbs. 

I'm unsure if No Man's Sky intended it to be this way or if the writing is just awful because of the limits of the 'language' system they've used for alien dialog (which makes no sense in the context of the actual universe, everyone clearly understands each other but you cannot understand them without forty-some hours of relic hunting to learn words one by one across three languages.) I'll spare you a break down of the awful writing and simply say that it seems intentional to allow the player to ignore the main quest (and all side-ventures, all of which make just as much sense and result in absolutely nothing for 'characters' you care nothing about.)

All-in-all No Man's Sky is the perfect couch game if you have four hours to kill, but be aware that it's best played blind (No guides, streams, etc.) but at the same time requires you to basically run the game alongside a web browser so you can google how to get half the damn equipment that has been added in since launch in 2018. Or how to change freighters. Or what the hell the multiplayer hub world is supposed to be. Or where to find some obscure thing required to craft some nonsense that a quest or object requires that can only be found on a blue star planet. 

Good luck.

Review is old but over time looking at it's update, I do believe it has become something worthwhile to pour in the time and be rewarded in it's own way.

OLD REVIEW:
The game has a lot of potential to be even more fun and exciting with friends but it still lacks something. Something beside the storyline. Something you do to reward yourself after all the grind to get better freighter, better multi-tool , better starship. 

Some yes points:

+ The game has done a wonderful job on improving it's graphical component. It looks so much better than it's first initial launch. 3rd person view is definitely a + , giving you option to appreciate your ship flying and your character animation.

+-The crafting system has a little more depth to it now that you have to process resources but at the core gameplay, it hasn't changed much. What is the core? Resource hoarding, inventory management, resource trading. 

+ The space station now is a lot wider and has more function as one. Allowing trades,blueprint , back pack upgrades and some mission browsing. 

+-You can build in your freighter now, but has no option to move build or transfer resource when buying a new freighter.

+ Multiplayer! 


Some rant:

・While the freighter works as a mobile base, it doesn't allow you to move items or move your builds when you buy a new freighter. You either move everything over manually or lose everything. 

The freighter does nothing else than be a travelling storage. If you encounter enemies near your freighter, your freighter would just watch as you get blown to bits. What are the weapons on them then!? As if they're purely weapons against player.

--If and when one of your team mate summon their freighter in the system. No one else can summon theirs. You need to either leave game session or move to a different system to summon your freighter.

・They implemented the fleet system. I liked it but I feel it is too shallow. Send them out to missions and wait for them to return and bring you some extra units. Nothing you can't make more on your own. And if the frigates do get damaged, you have to bring materials over manually to repair each of the frigates one by one. You're the captain of the goddamned fleet, not some repairman FFS. Why can't you just send materials, command the fleet to do their job!?

・Perhaps a level system for weapons and starship to improve beyond what you own so engaging sentinels would make more sense. Otherwise, avoiding them would save a lot more trouble. Things like finding/buying ship parts and customizing the ship on your own and raising the rank of your ship than to actively find a ship you like/want.

Spent a few million units to buy that ship with bigger inventory and cooler look? Oh look another ship with even better inventory and appearance. Too bad you ran out of funds. 

・The character customization is really nice but if they're implemented as treasures you find/unlock. Wouldn't it add more depth to things you could do? Something to be rewarded with exploring depth of caves or abandoned bases. Rather than just materials. Something built to be used right away. Something to reward you directly for going through all the trouble to zip here and there to look for stuff. 

・If you decline the story mission at the start from atlas. You literally do not get the blueprint to build the seals to repair. You are ultimately left to die and with no means to progress or repair unless stumble upon a built one somewhere with enough luck.


★Conclusion: The game hasn't really changed much from before. The "NEXT" update just added more obstacle for you to achieve something, a fucking lot more. The core gameplay hasn't really changed. For an exploration game. There is very little need for exploring. Zoom in, get what you need , zoom out. Fuck all. 

★Impression: I enjoyed the game 2 years ago and still did with the NEXT update but it didn't really last. I really enjoyed base building . Travelling to find cool planets, earth-like planets to settle in. The game has a grand scale but what you do in the game has so little impact in both story and world. Sure , atlas path can be " huge impact " but it's basically new game+ and you don't get rewarded on that. 

The NEXT update has only done what it said to do 2 years ago. Hope to see actual revolutionary updates and new mechanics to the game in the future. As of, 28th July 2018. The game is buggy as hell. Saves file gets corrupted and the time invested in it. ALL GONE. 

Wouldn't really recommend the game as of now. Perhaps when they implement more in-depth changes to the core gameplay.

Next and Beyond were great updates with a lot of promising ideas. Beyond, in particular, took NMS to a whole other level. But then, the following updates kept on introducing new features without addressing existing content.

Desolation, the update that came out just a few days ago, is yet another content drop that adds a compelling idea that's completely disjointed from the rest of the game, much like everything else. The shift in tone from the usually chill space exploration is a breath of fresh air and exploring the derelict freighters is quite intriguing. 

Until you realize the procedural generation can only go so far. On my second run, I was already growing tired of the "unique" stories surrounding each freighter, all of which consist of quite a lot of things going wrong, none of it having anything to do with the crew disappearing, and oh—yeah, they're all gone. The freighters are also identical outside and inside, which is quite disappointing considering the variation in usable freighters and crashed ones. 

While No Man's Sky in 2020 (and beyond) really is a massive improvement over its catastrophic 2016 release, it is now a collection of features that have little to nothing to do with one another. The stories they added are far from interesting, especially when they have a laser focus on exploration but there's nothing interesting to see after you've visited two or three systems at the beginning of your journey. There's quite a lot to keep one occupied but for the most part, none of it is engaging.

They really need to stop developing so much new content and rework the game once again. There are just too many features that need some attention right now and some of them were even added recently (e.g. the random space encounters, most of which are underwhelming and add nothing to the core gameplay besides stopping you to look at something that's rarely worth stopping for).

Might still be worth getting when it's on sale if you've never played it, but don't expect to be blown away. Until they overhaul older features and take more recent ones somewhere (and also bother to tie seemingly correlating features together, which is not the case right now), this isn't worth the hype. 

There are cheaper games that will give you a much more fulfilling experience in fewer hours. I played over 300h of NMS since Atlas Rises but that playtime feels unfulfilling when most of it was spent just seeing what they added, building a base, and then getting bored cuz there's nothing engaging about the game, not even the few multiplayer features, which are probably the most disjointed of the bunch.

I've gone through lots of ups and downs with this game. I've both defended it and criticized it, citing all the usual things about missing features and broken promises. I've written and rewritten this review, changing it from Recommended to Not Recommended, and back to Recommended again. I've uninstalled it so many times, thinking I'd never go back to it. But in the end, I always did, and here's why.

No other game I've ever played has ever given me the experience that No Man's Sky has. The freedom that the game gives the player to explore is something that I've never experienced in any other game. Probably my favorite thing to do in the game right now is land on a new planet, scan some plants for easy cash, and take some awesome pictures of the landscapes which, with the new and improved graphics, almost always look amazing. I have seen mountains, valleys, lakes and oceans beautiful enough to take your breath away and then gone over the hill or to a new planet to see a few more entirely different vistas (and pick up some sweet loot along the way). Granted, sometimes I want something a bit more goal-oriented, so I do the in-game missions, upgrade my ship or suit, expand my base (or build a new one) or explore some of the game's new features that are constantly being added in substantial content updates. It's a relaxing, sometimes almost meditative experience where I can just be in the moment exploring some beautiful new world, something I've never gotten from any other game.

This is not to say the game is without problems. The story has been fleshed out a bit but the ending wasn't really satisfying (for me at least), the inventory system is improved but can still be a bit clunky and difficult to navigate (even for someone who's been playing with it since launch) and there are still bugs and performance issues that crop up now and again, most commonly in multiplayer encounters. But none of these things take away from the overall experience of the game for me and, on top of that, Hello Games's consistent support over the game over the past 4 years since launch shows no signs of stopping, so I am sure that these issues will be addressed.

If you at all think you would enjoy any of the things I described here, I encourage you to pick up this game. If you think that experience is worth $60, pick it up today! If not, wait until it goes on sale (it usually drops to around $30 whenever a new update is released) and pick it up then. I don't think you'll regret it. I definitely don't!

I would be writing a different review if this update was garbage, or if they never touched the game again. But now that their development strategy has become more apparent to me. I can see the potential of launching a game that is a mile wide and an inch deep, and then simply adding inches as the outrage and feedback flows in. 

Excellent update. As effective in salvaging the game as Diablo 3's overhaul. At this rate, with an update this big every 3 months. The value of the game is going to multiply. Simply because any feature + infinite planets creates a huge yeild of gameplay potential. The survival mode is superbly difficult and forces you to utilize everything to get by. Huge improvement there for me. The one bug im having is with the look acceleration when in flight (edit: i just had to update the lowflight mod). But because the combat isn't important it isn't breaking the game for me. Which bring me to my next point:

UPDATE THE COMBAT NEXT!!!

I think the game isn't perfect, the hyping was badly handled, basic things like "return to main menu" don't exist in the game. But it has been worth it for ME. 
I think that a flat price of $60 for the game, the whole game and nothing but the game is a better way to monetize than, kickstart donations, microtransactions, subscriptions and paid dlc.
HG selling their game at a flat price, even if it's $30 too high, they don't deserve the level of hate that the gaming community have unleashed on them.

As a student of game development i can see right through the Molyneux speak as a necessary part of gaming enthusiasm. I guarantee if you try to make a game the first thing you will do is pitch the idea to colleagues, and as you pitch it to them you will propose countless features that you can't code for or that nobody can code for. 
When they ask Sean about multiplayer and he winces and talks about the improbability, as a developer i can see he wants it, but can't imagine how to implement it. Then ppl take it as OMG INFINITE SCALE MULTIPLAYER CONFIRMED! This is exactly like that scene from Dumb & Dumber, where she says "one in a million" and he exclaims "SO THERE"S STILL A CHANCE!" 

I recommend the game to anyone who's looked at the game being played and is still interested. It's no better or worse than how it seems when you watch a game stream. A game can be incomplete but still very solid and unique, whilst a complete game can be a real peice of crap. 
For example, not that it's a piece of crap but the recent Doom game, it also released at full price. I was very close to getting it, i watch some game stream of it. Reviews.183529:
(OLD RELEASE REVIEW AT BOTTOM)
I have to hand it to Hello Games. They committed to turning this game around and making it something worthwhile, and everything I've seen so far points to that being an achievable goal. The sheer mass of content in the game now fills in a lot of the massive gameplay gaps hidden under the pretty aesthetics. Is it a total turn around? Not yet, but this now feels like a pleasant mix of space opera and base building that's definitely worthy of its current pricing.

I hope that HG stick at it and can turn their reputation around, as there's obviously some talented and passionate people working there that are willing to fix their mistakes instead of abandoning a project and rushing to a new one.

((Imagine a giant, shiny paddle pool, the size of a galaxy, but so shallow its barely ankle deep. Throw in some food coloring to and shiny ornaments to get that whole aesthetic crowd on side with the pretty trailers. Imagine promising the world, but make sure none of the promises are concrete enough to be legally binding. Imagine a world where every activity you can perform is of the minimal required detail that it can still be considered a feature.))

That just about sums up my thoughts on NMS. Its a game that looks great on a list of bullet points, because even if you take out the disputed content such as multiplayer and the like, and you'll have a long list of various things that can be done in the game. The issue arises when you scrutinize any one feature of the game. Without fail, every activity you can perform in NMS feels like the minimum amount of effort was put in.

To make a point (ahem,) Ill lay out criticisms of the features as bullet points!

- Exploration is little more than wandering a vast, fundamentally flat planet, scanning the occasional new rock or plant, for little reward other than ticking off a checklist.

- Combat seems to revolve around shooting one of a handful of very low intelligence enemies, (Only encountered two types of planetside enemy in my entire playtime)

- Quests are a joke, little more than a single paragraph of dialog, and a multiple choice question.

- Customization has literally no effect visually on any of your equipment, they are little more than trading cards you put in slots. Half of the abilities arent even needed since they are to do with combat, and all enemies can be easily dispatched by the standard weapon types. About all you need to worry about is making some power upgrades to you basic gun and beam.

- Resource gathering Is a lot like combat, only you shoot inanimate objects. Honestly feeling like just another way to drag out what little content there is by making you busy yourself lasering the same lump of metal for 10 minutes straight.

- Crafting is very tied to the customization. Therefore all you craft are the little slottable trading cards, the importance of which I've already covered. The only really essential parts are gated behind certain items you need to craft them.

- Space feels even less developed than planetside. The bare minimum of a space shooter, where shooting the space enemies is entirely optional, and not even remotely rewarding. 

- Story is bordering on non-existent. An early choice that has been proven by brave (ie extraordinarily patient) players to be inconsequential to the outcome of the game. Basically just a line of the so-called quests that string together the content gates you have to craft to get to more of the same content.

- Online is one of the most contentious issues on the entire game. The ability to identify, name, and share the info on content you discover in the game would have been revolutionary, if SPORE hadnt come out 8 years ago, and do the same thing better, including adding your own custom content to the game universe.

- Trading I almost forgot to make comment on, as it was horribly useless. Mostly you use it as a way to sell excess resources. If youre really desperate, you can jump between trading terminals in hope of getting a slightly higher prices, but the returns don't make up for the time wasted and the resources spent on the travel.

- Ships were the biggest personal disappointment of the game. All of them handle -exactly- the same. The looks are completely costmetic, with the only statistic of any import on each ship being the number of slots. More always being better, with no compromises to be made. I did like the prospect of finding crashed ships to repair out in the field, however, due to the way the game scales content, you're highly unlikely to find a wreck with more slots than the ship you have, making wrecks mostly useless.

- Taming isn't even a thing, you can give some animals a resource, and they might randomly dig you up some other resource.

- The tools you find are basically the same as ships, more slots equals better, without fail, no need to decide on pros and cons, just grab more slots.

In the end, the comparison to SPORE is a good one. Another game that promised a lot and let down many of its fans with the end result. The difference is that the depth of content, and just the sheer personality of the game gave it some merits.

TL;DR - NMS is a masterpiece of putting in the bare minimum content needed to rake in the pre-purchases, and dragging said content out long enough that hopefully most players pass the refund threshold on steam.

The game has come an EXTREMELY long way since it released back in 2016, I mean a LONG way.  There have been 80+ updates to the game, across 12 MAJOR content releases. ***Original Review***

****There are some indirect spoilers in this review move on if you don't want any Skip Reading this review***

To quote the "credits" page of NMS own Dev website ([url=no-mans-sky.com/press/sheet.php?p=credits]Link to source[/url]) "...A good game is worth nothing if no-one plays it..."  Base on the overwhelming # of negative reviews for this game the game should be worth very little...

Having 80 hours in the game I've hit a wall, I love what I see, I see soooooo much potential for a very very fun exploration/survival game here, even if it stays simgleplayer forever...but at this point all of the tech I find I already know, I have a inventory with 40+ slots in it and a spaceship, I found at a crashsite, with the max # of inventory slots as well.  And sadly i've only explored about 6-7 worlds.

Miles wide (light-years even), inch deep for sure.  I do not agree with the posts that say that people were promised multiplayer, I knew over a year ago this was not going to be a EVE, Elite, or SC type game where you could meet up with friends and play together (I can site sources for that info if needed, reply in to this review and I'll update).  

I do think that there needs to be more content to the game, a LOT more.  Having a handful of base materials that are used to craft all of the other rarer items makes the game VERY grindy.  The fact that I cannot make a warp cell directly when I have the base mats to make the components in my inventory is adding to that grindiness as well. I'm fine with only 3-4 factions (if you count the atlas).  The Stack size limits need to be increased, across the board.  Make fewer items single stack items, or increase the slot limits across the board.  Beefy up the space adventure side of things, more random events, more diverse pre fabs, etc.

Get on with the content updates that were promised on release day, and keep going.  

Word of warning to the Devs, avoid the mistakes made by other devs recently, read Wildcard Studios (ARK), do not put out a paid DLC for this game, at least not until the game gets a LOT more content in the base game, unless you want to ramp up the rage machine you kicked off with this content lacking intial release.

Desert planets

Reviews.196213:
Hello Games have finally redeemed themselves after many years. No Man's Sky has definitely improved to be worthy of a thumbs up review. Well done.

======================================================================

No Man's Sky shows some amazing potential. It has a grand vision and a solid foundation for something great. But in the end that's all this game really is...amazing potential.

The first 10-20 hours will be magical: a new planet flourishing with seemingly unique plant life and animals, resources to gather, a spaceship, once fixed, will be your portal to explore the vast cosmos. Look up in the sky and see other planets and possibly even moons that you can actually fly to and claim discovery like Christopher Columbus. It all seems like a fantasy come true.

Then reality strikes...

The front page of the No Man's Sky Steam store showcases some blatant lies.

For example, the page says [i]"In this infinite procedurally generated universe, you'll discover places and creatures that no other players have seen before - and perhaps never will again."[/i]

That is a flat lie.

After about hour 20 where you should have a few hyper space jumps under your belt and have explored each planet and moon in the systems where you have visited, you come to the realization that the places and creatures you discover have some extreme likenesses, and in fact are exactly the same places and creatures that you have visited on previous planets.

The same plants, the same animals, the same buildings, the same life forms, the same space stations, the same ships, the same weather patterns, the same sentinels. It's ALL the same.

Everything is a clone of everything else, just on an immensely vast scale.

[i]"At the centre of the galaxy lies a irresistible pulse which draws you on a journey towards it to learn the true nature of the cosmos."[/i]

This statement isn't even worth dissecting. It is just not true.

[i]"But, facing hostile creatures and fierce pirates, you'll know that death comes at a cost, and survival will be down to the choices you make over how you upgrade your ship, your weapon and suit."[/i]

Death doesn't come at a cost; you simply respawn and go to your grave to get your stuff back. Unless you consider choosing not to recharge your life support as a choice for survival, there are really no choices to make that affect your survival.

[i]"Trade convoys travel between stars"[/i]

No.

[i]"Factions vie for territory"[/i]

No.

Mind you, I've taken these statements directly from the No Man's Sky Steam store page. I have not edited them in any shape, form, or fashion. They are just flat lies.

Then there was the promises by Sean Murray in his many videos about the features that this game would offer. Blatant lies and false promises. Certainly stretching the truth at a minimum. Stephen Colbert was even genuinely amazed and excited.

And then there's that multiplayer thing....that isn't quite multiplayer. More like an online catalog.

The final nail in the coffin of this terrific alpha build is its instability and crashes. No finished game should ever crash this much. EVER. And it's not even one game breaking bug. There are literally dozens of game breaking bugs. Nearly every action in the game has been tied to a crash. Hello Games has no respect for quality assurance. They've hyped up the product feeding on the hopes and dreams of anyone willing to drink the koolaid. Unfortunately they've laced that koolaid with cyanide...

No Man's Sky is ultimately a product launch failure, but it might be the most profitable failure of all time. Outside of the excessive crashing, I enjoyed the first 20ish hours. But boasting 18 quintillion planets, I expected a lot more variety and uniqueness that would continually keep the exploration and discovery aspects fresh and exciting. Instead the game hits a point where it feels empty, mundane, and downright boring.
